survey.agentChannel:
EXISTING AGENT JSON CHANNEL — exact shape, all citations absolute.

TRANSPORT. TCP, newline-delimited JSON, one JSON object per line, no request ids. Mac: /Users/you/Desktop/SolStream/macos/SolStreamClient/Sources/StreamConnection/AgentConnection.swift:715-736 (send appends 0x0A at :726) and :764-791 (drainLines splits on 0x0A). Host: /Users/you/Desktop/SolStream/windows/SolStreamAgent/main.cpp:3072-3088 (SendLine appends '\n', serialised by g_send_cs) and :3312-3382 (recv loop, splits on '\n', strips trailing '\r').

REPLY MATCHING IS POSITIONAL, NOT ID'D. AgentConnection.swift:117-118 keeps a FIFO of continuations; handle() pops exactly one per non-push reply (AgentConnection.swift:913-918). One unparseable line desynchronises everything after it, so the Mac drops the connection rather than misroute (AgentConnection.swift:769-780). The host mirrors this: an oversized line still emits exactly one error reply, "zero or two desynchronises every later reply" (main.cpp:3371-3381).

LINE CAPS. kMaxLineBytes = 4 MiB, kMaxClipboardBytes = 256 KiB (main.cpp:80-81); mirrored on the Mac at AgentConnection.swift:478-479 with the note that the two must move together.

AUTH. Shared secret = 16 bytes from BCryptGenRandom rendered as 32 lowercase hex chars (main.cpp:1257-1271), persisted at %LOCALAPPDATA%\SolStream\agent.token (main.cpp:1247-1255), compared in constant time (main.cpp:1311-1322). Wrong token costs a deliberate Sleep(1000) (main.cpp:2790-2795). g_require_auth is true unless bound to loopback (main.cpp:3733); --no-auth is refused off loopback (main.cpp:3722-3728). The channel is PLAINTEXT TCP — main.cpp:1239-1242 states explicitly that this authenticates the client to the host and does nothing else: no confidentiality, no protection from a reader of the traffic.

HANDSHAKE SEQUENCE (host speaks first, unprompted):
1. {"type":"hello","version":1,"host":"<computername>","needsAuth":true|false,"sunshineInstance":"<u64>"} — main.cpp:3280-3286; kProtocolVersion = 1 at main.cpp:70. sunshineInstance is pid XOR process-creation-FILETIME, 0 when Sunshine is not running (main.cpp:3098-3138).
2. If needsAuth, the Mac sends {"cmd":"auth","token":"…"} outside the FIFO (AgentConnection.swift:387-396) and the host replies {"type":"auth","ok":true} / {"ok":false,"message":"bad token"} (main.cpp:2783-2795). If the Mac holds a token and the host says needsAuth:false, the Mac treats that as impersonation and drops without reconnecting (AgentConnection.swift:839-850).
3. The host then pushes the display list — withheld until authenticated so the monitor layout does not leak (main.cpp:3289-3310, 3356-3361).

COMMANDS (dispatch: main.cpp HandleCommand at :2740-3065).
- ping → {"type":"pong"} — answered BEFORE auth (main.cpp:2752-2754). Mac heartbeats it every 10 s (AgentConnection.swift:198, 283-294) because the host drops a client idle for 30 s (main.cpp:3266-3267, 3320-3323).
- status → answered BEFORE auth (main.cpp:2760-2778): {"sunshine":"running|starting|failed|missing|stopped","sunshineDetail","basePort","captureDisplay","virtualDisplay"}.
- auth (above).
- displays → {"type":"displays","displays":[{name,adapter,x,y,w,h,primary,captured}]} (main.cpp:2438-2467; parsed AgentConnection.swift:935-947). `captured` is authoritative: it names the display Sunshine is actually encoding.
- windows → {"type":"windows","windows":[{id,pid,title,class,x,y,w,h,exStyle,captionInset,occluded,occludedBy?}]} (main.cpp:2469-2495). x/y/w/h are the CLIENT AREA in virtual-desktop coordinates (AgentConnection.swift:41-48). NOTE: exStyle is emitted (main.cpp:2483) and silently dropped by the Swift parser (AgentConnection.swift:949-961).
- apps → {"type":"apps","apps":[{name,path}]} from Start Menu .lnk files; the reply also seeds the launch/icon allowlist (main.cpp:2810-2816).
- clipboard → get {"cmd":"clipboard","seq":N} returns {"ok","seq","unchanged"} or text; set {"cmd":"clipboard","text":"…"} (main.cpp:2818-2832). Mac polls every 1.0 s (ClipboardBridge.swift:42).
- icon {id|path} → {"ok","w","h","bgra":<base64>} raw un-premultiplied BGRA, no image codec on either end (main.cpp:2834-2860; AgentConnection.swift:527-559).
- canvas — see below.
- pair {"pin","name"} → the agent posts the PIN to Sunshine's own local API so no browser is involved (main.cpp:2887-2912).
- window {id} → {"alive","minimized","x","y","w","h","captionInset","occluded","occludedBy"} (main.cpp:2515-2560). Mac polls every 1.0 s (AppWindow.swift:139).
- launch {path,timeoutMs} → BLOCKS on the host until a window appears, clamped 1000–60000 ms (main.cpp:2922-2945). Only allowlisted apps.
- place {id,x,y,w,h} → {"type":"placed","ok","x","y","w","h","minW","minH","border"} (main.cpp:2947-2973).
- lock {id,on} / topmost {id,on} / focus {id} → {"type":"locked"/"topmost"/"focused","ok",…} (main.cpp:2975-3062).

UNSOLICITED PUSHES (must not consume a FIFO slot — AgentConnection.swift:818-911): hello, the first displays, cursor {"shape":"…"} (host pushes on change; cursor watcher polls at 40 ms, main.cpp:3206/3228), closed {"id"}, occluded {"id","by"} (debounced host-side), windowsChanged (a nudge with no payload; window watcher ticks every 120 ms, main.cpp:1962), busy, auth.

CANVAS — WHAT IT ACTUALLY NEGOTIATES. {"cmd":"canvas","display":<DXGI device name>,"w":W,"h":H} → {"type":"canvas","ok":true,"w":got,"h":got,"hz":got} (main.cpp:2862-2885; AgentConnection.swift:606-617). Range-checked 640x480 … 8192x8192 (main.cpp:2869-2871). It is NOT a stream renegotiation: SetDisplayMode (main.cpp:416-495) only SWITCHES between modes the display driver already enumerates — smallest mode covering the request, highest refresh among equals — via ChangeDisplaySettingsExW with CDS_UPDATEREGISTRY. Adding modes needs a device restart and is done once at setup. hz is returned so the Mac can log a display stuck at 30 Hz, which otherwise looks exactly like a slow network (main.cpp:2879-2880).

The Mac asks for its own screen in pixels (NSScreen.frame × backingScaleFactor), clamped to 4096 (main.swift:417-423), and ONLY for a virtual display — a real monitor is somebody's actual screen (main.swift:439-444). After a successful canvas the Mac re-enumerates displays because a mode change can move the origin (main.swift:461-469).

SESSION START TODAY. The agent channel does NOT start the media session. StreamConnection does it entirely over Sunshine's own ports: HTTP pairing → HTTPS /launch or /resume with a 16-byte random `rikey` (hex) and mode=WxHxFPS (StreamConnection.swift:614-680) → RTSP OPTIONS, DESCRIBE, SETUP audio, SETUP video, SETUP control, ANNOUNCE, PLAY (StreamConnection.swift:684-762). The agent's only involvement is `pair` (PIN injection) and `canvas` (display mode). The rikey doubles as the AES-128-GCM key for the control channel (StreamConnection.swift:185-186, ControlStream.swift:41-44). A new transport deriving keys from the agent session would replace all of this.

WHAT THE CLIENT KNOWS ABOUT THE HOST BEFORE ANY MEDIA FLOWS: computer name, protocol version, whether auth is needed, the Sunshine instance id, Sunshine's run state and base port, the capture display's device name, whether a virtual display exists, the full display list with which one is captured, the window list with client rects and caption insets, the launchable app list, and per-window minimum size and resize-border width from `place`.

payloadTypes.name: Video: coded picture data (currently whole-frame, 1 slice/frame)
payloadTypes.typicalBytes: Per datagram TODAY: 1040 bytes total = 32-byte header + 1008-byte payload. Derived from Config.packetSize = 1024 (StreamConnection.swift:44), blocksize = packetSize + 16 and payloadBlocksize = blocksize - 32 (Tests/SolStreamClientTests/ProtocolTests.swift:15,30-31), VideoDepacketizer.headerSize = 32 (VideoDepacketizer.swift:40). NOTE A CONTRADICTION IN-TREE: the Config doc comment says the datagram is packetSize 'plus a 16-byte header' (StreamConnection.swift:34-35) while the depacketizer and the tests both use 32. Per frame: no measurement exists in the repo. Arithmetic from the configured defaults (1920x1080, 60 fps, 20000 kbps — StreamConnection.swift:43-45) gives ~41.7 KB average per frame, ~42 datagrams; IDR frames are 'several times the size of a P-frame' (ControlStream.swift:103-104) but no number is recorded anywhere.
payloadTypes.rate: 60 fps configured (StreamConnection.swift:43-45); ~2500 datagrams/s at the default bitrate. --packet-size overrides the payload for smaller-MTU links (main.swift:59-67); the code notes Tailscale/WireGuard links are 1280 (StreamConnection.swift:35).
payloadTypes.ordering: Reorder-tolerant within a frame — shards are keyed by index in a dictionary (VideoDepacketizer.swift:203-208). Frame boundaries are strictly increasing: a lower frame index is rejected as stale, with a 96-packet resync escape hatch for the /resume case where two encoders share the socket (VideoDepacketizer.swift:67, 150-169). Duplicates are dropped (first shard wins, VideoDepacketizer.swift:205).
payloadTypes.notes: The existing SDP explicitly asks for videoEncoderSlicesPerFrame:1 and maxNumReferenceFrames:1 and intraRefresh:0 (StreamConnection.swift:789-790, 814) — i.e. the current path is the opposite of the slice-streaming, LTR, intra-refresh design being specified. fec.enable:1 is also requested (StreamConnection.swift:803) and the parity shards are received and discarded (VideoDepacketizer.swift:139-142), so FEC bandwidth is being paid for and thrown away today.

payloadTypes.name: Video: parameter sets (SPS/PPS)
payloadTypes.typicalBytes: Tens of bytes each. Not separately framed — they arrive in-band inside the frame's Annex-B stream ahead of every IDR (VideoDecoder.swift:17-19).
payloadTypes.rate: Once per IDR. IDR cadence is not configured anywhere in SolStream's code; it is Sunshine's default plus explicit requests.
payloadTypes.ordering: Must precede the first picture NAL the decoder is asked to decode, or nothing can be built.
payloadTypes.notes: The decoder cannot start without them and re-asks for an IDR every 0.5 s until it has them (VideoDecoder.swift:35, 107-120). A new transport must guarantee parameter sets reach a joining/recovering receiver — this is the single hard ordering requirement in the video path.

payloadTypes.name: Audio: Opus packet
payloadTypes.typicalBytes: No measurement in the repo. Frame duration is negotiated as 5 ms (a=x-nv-aqos.packetDuration:5, StreamConnection.swift:807), 48 kHz stereo (OpusDecoder.swift:12-13, AudioRenderer.swift:18-20). Today each datagram carries a 12-byte RTP header plus the Opus payload (StreamSession.swift:296, 302).
payloadTypes.rate: ~200 packets/s — stated in-code as 'roughly 200 times a second' (StreamSession.swift:242-243).
payloadTypes.ordering: Sequence-numbered; a gap resets the Opus decoder so it does not interpolate across it (StreamSession.swift:287-294). Out-of-order or lost frames are simply dropped — 'a gap is inaudible' at 5 ms (StreamSession.swift:271-277).
payloadTypes.notes: Audio parity shards (payload type 127) are received and discarded; audio payload type is 97 (StreamSession.swift:302-304). Audio is NOT encrypted today (StreamSession.swift:277-278). Opus decoding on the Mac is AudioToolbox kAudioFormatOpus, not libopus — no third-party audio dependency exists on the Mac side at all (OpusDecoder.swift:1-9, 34-64).

payloadTypes.name: Media keepalive / path establishment ping
payloadTypes.typicalBytes: 20 bytes: 16-byte ASCII payload from X-SS-Ping-Payload + 4-byte big-endian sequence (UdpStream.swift:210-222).
payloadTypes.rate: Every 500 ms per media socket, video and audio staggered by 250 ms (UdpStream.swift:111-117; StreamConnection.swift:986).
payloadTypes.notes: This is how the host learns where to send: it latches the source address of the ping, so pings MUST leave the same socket that receives the media (UdpStream.swift:5-12). The staggering exists because two pings landing in one reactor cycle made the host record one stream's port for the other (UdpStream.swift:62-70). Any replacement transport needs an equivalent explicit path-establishment step and must survive NAT rebinding — see constraints.

payloadTypes.name: Input: key down / key up
payloadTypes.typicalBytes: 14 bytes built (8-byte header + 6-byte payload: flags:1, keycode LE:2, modifiers:1, zero:2 — InputProtocol.swift:103-110, 144-151). On the wire today it is wrapped in the encrypted control envelope: 2+2+4 header + 16-byte tag + AES-GCM over (type:2 + len:2 + payload) = 42 bytes, plus ENet framing (ControlStream.swift:387-436).
payloadTypes.rate: Human typing — bursts to a few tens per second. Auto-repeat is Windows-side.
payloadTypes.ordering: STRICTLY ORDERED AND MUST NOT BE LOST. A keydown delivered after its keyup is a stuck key, and the host auto-repeats a key it never sees released (InputCapture.swift:169-171). The client already carries explicit compensating machinery for this: heldKeys/chordKeys released on focus loss (InputCapture.swift:329-350), chord release when Command goes up because macOS does not reliably deliver key-up under ⌘ (InputCapture.swift:266-271, 313-324), and dedup for the two physical keys that map to one Windows VK (InputCapture.swift:135-142).
payloadTypes.notes: Carried on its own ENet channel (keyboard = 2) precisely so a lost mouse-move cannot stall a keystroke behind it (InputProtocol.swift:112-140). Key codes are Windows virtual-key codes; ⌘ is mapped to Ctrl and the Windows key is deliberately unreachable (InputCapture.swift:99-124).

payloadTypes.name: Input: mouse move (absolute)
payloadTypes.typicalBytes: 18 bytes built (8-byte header + 5 × Int16: x, y, unused, refWidth-1, refHeight-1 — InputProtocol.swift:61-71). ~46 bytes inside the current encrypted envelope.
payloadTypes.rate: One packet per NSEvent — there is NO coalescing in the capture layer (InputCapture.swift:384-389). macOS delivers mouse-moved at the pointing device's rate; no measured number exists in the repo. Suppressed entirely during a live window resize (InputCapture.swift:378-381, 386-395).
payloadTypes.ordering: Order matters only in that the last position wins; intermediate positions are droppable. This is the one input class where coalescing/newest-wins is correct.
payloadTypes.notes: Coordinates are sent in CANVAS pixels with the reference rectangle attached, so the host rescales and the Mac's crop is invisible to it (InputCapture.swift:14-19, 429-473). An edgeGuard inset keeps the host pointer off the window's own resize border (InputCapture.swift:22-31, 515-523); its width comes back from the `place` reply as `border`.

payloadTypes.name: Input: mouse button down / up
payloadTypes.typicalBytes: 9 bytes built (8-byte header + 1 button byte — InputProtocol.swift:81-83).
payloadTypes.ordering: STRICTLY ORDERED AND MUST NOT BE LOST, and ordered relative to the mouse-move that precedes it — a button-down is always preceded by a position because Windows clicks wherever the pointer is (InputCapture.swift:391-402). A lost button-up leaves a rubber-band selection or a permanent drag (InputCapture.swift:176-180).

payloadTypes.name: Input: scroll (vertical / horizontal)
payloadTypes.typicalBytes: 14 bytes vertical (three Int16), 10 bytes horizontal (one Int16) — InputProtocol.swift:86-100.
payloadTypes.rate: Trackpad scrolling produces a dense burst; wheel produces one per detent.
payloadTypes.ordering: Ordered but individually droppable; amounts accumulate on the host.
payloadTypes.notes: Units are Windows wheel clicks × 120; the Mac scales trackpad points by 12 and wheel lines by 120 (InputCapture.swift:411-422).

payloadTypes.name: Feedback: keyframe / IDR request
payloadTypes.typicalBytes: Empty payload; 8 bytes built, ~40 on the wire in the current envelope (ControlStream.swift:272).
payloadTypes.rate: Hard-limited to one per 500 ms on the sending side (ControlStream.swift:35, 105-120) because an unthrottled request storm makes loss worse — IDRs are large, so loss produced a bandwidth spike which produced more loss.
payloadTypes.ordering: Idempotent; a duplicate costs an extra IDR, a lost one is retried by the next tick.
payloadTypes.notes: THIS IS THE ONLY FEEDBACK THE MAC SENDS TODAY. Three independent producers ask for it: the depacketizer on an incomplete frame (StreamConnection.swift:962-964), the decoder when it has no parameter sets or hit a recoverable VT error (VideoDecoder.swift:114-118, 219-227), and the session watchdog after 1 s of no frames, up to 5 times before declaring the stream lost (StreamSession.swift:90-94, 184-225). Sent on ENet channel 1 ('urgent').

payloadTypes.name: Feedback: loss report / receive rate / bitrate control
payloadTypes.typicalBytes: DOES NOT EXIST. A lossStats packet type (0x0201) is declared at ControlStream.swift:23 and is never constructed or sent anywhere in the tree (grep across Sources returns only the declaration).
payloadTypes.notes: Bitrate is fixed for the session: min and max are both set to config.bitrateKbps in the ANNOUNCE SDP (StreamConnection.swift:801-802), default 20000 kbps. There is no adaptation loop of any kind. The counters that a rate controller would need do exist locally and unused: bytesReceived/packetsReceived per socket (UdpStream.swift:31-36), framesDelivered/framesDropped/packetsStale/packetsParity (VideoDepacketizer.swift:76-88), audio frames and gaps (StreamSession.swift:59-61).

payloadTypes.name: Feedback: round-trip time
payloadTypes.direction: measurement, no packet of its own
payloadTypes.rate: Sampled once per control-loop tick, i.e. at worst every 50 ms (ControlStream.swift:223, 232-234).
payloadTypes.notes: Taken from ENet's own reliable-packet RTT estimate rather than measured by SolStream, because the media pings are never echoed (ControlStream.swift:64-73). It is surfaced in the UI as 'latency' (QualityPill.swift:111) and in the stats line. A replacement transport must produce this number itself — nothing else in the tree measures RTT.

payloadTypes.name: Control keepalive
payloadTypes.notes: Exists because the host kills a session whose control channel goes quiet for 10 s and only refreshes that deadline on a real message — transport-level keep-alives do not count (ControlStream.swift:8-13).

payloadTypes.name: Session lifecycle: start / terminate
payloadTypes.typicalBytes: START_A 0x0305 and START_B 0x0307, 4-byte payloads, sent on connect (ControlStream.swift:238-245). TERMINATION 0x0109, 4-byte payload, sent on teardown and flushed (ControlStream.swift:288-291); inbound termination carries a 4-byte reason code (ControlStream.swift:337-346).
payloadTypes.ordering: Must arrive. Teardown deliberately blocks up to 0.4 s to get TERMINATION on the wire (StreamConnection.swift:328-329) and then ALSO calls HTTPS /cancel as belt and braces, because TERMINATION alone leaves the host reporting BUSY and locking out every later client (StreamConnection.swift:332-338).
payloadTypes.notes: There is no renegotiate message at all. The canvas is fixed for the life of the session — 'mode= is negotiated at /launch and ANNOUNCE, so changing it later would mean tearing the session down and reconnecting' (main.swift:562-566). A Mac window resize therefore resizes the HOST WINDOW inside a fixed canvas via the agent's `place`, not the stream. Reconnect on the media path does not exist; StreamSession cannot be restarted in place and recovery means closing the windows and building a new session (main.swift:616-620).

payloadTypes.name: Cursor shape
payloadTypes.typicalBytes: One JSON line naming a standard cursor, e.g. {"type":"cursor","shape":"ibeam"}.
payloadTypes.rate: On change only; the host polls its own cursor at 40 ms (main.cpp:3206, 3228).
payloadTypes.notes: Carried on the AGENT TCP channel today, not on any media channel (AgentConnection.swift:862-868). It is pushed rather than polled because the agent serves one command at a time on one thread, so a poll fast enough to feel immediate would sit in front of every `place` sent during a live resize (main.cpp:3140-3151). Worth knowing when deciding what belongs on the new transport versus the existing JSON channel.

survey.decodePath:
WHAT THE MAC'S DECODE PATH EXPECTS TO BE HANDED.

THE HANDOFF STRUCT. `VideoFrame { frameIndex: UInt32, frameType: UInt8, annexB: Data }` (/Users/you/Desktop/SolStream/macos/SolStreamClient/Sources/StreamConnection/VideoDepacketizer.swift:5-13). frameType values documented there: 1 = P, 2 = IDR, 4 = intra-refresh, 5 = post-invalidation P; only `isIDR` (== 2) is read by anything (StreamSession.swift:123).

WIRE FORM EXPECTED: ANNEX-B, ONE COMPLETE ACCESS UNIT PER CALL. `VideoDecoder.decode(_ annexB: Data, isIDR: Bool)` (VideoDecoder.swift:74). It splits on 3- and 4-byte start codes (VideoDecoder.swift:162-194), classifies each NAL by `nal[0] & 0x1F` — 7 = SPS, 8 = PPS, 6/9/12 (SEI, AUD, filler) discarded, everything else is picture data (VideoDecoder.swift:85-97) — and then CONVERTS TO AVCC: each picture NAL is prefixed with its 4-byte big-endian length (VideoDecoder.swift:124-128), matching `nalUnitHeaderLength: 4` in the format description (VideoDecoder.swift:250). VideoToolbox will not accept Annex-B; feeding it raw makes the decoder read 00 00 00 01 as a 1-byte NAL and produce nothing (VideoDecoder.swift:11-15).

PARAMETER SETS ARE IN-BAND AND MANDATORY. The format description is built from SPS+PPS pulled out of the stream itself — no SDP parsing (VideoDecoder.swift:17-19, 232-262). Until both are present nothing decodes and an IDR is requested every 0.5 s (VideoDecoder.swift:103-120). The session is rebuilt when the parameter sets change OR when `session == nil`, deliberately, because a VideoToolbox session can be invalidated by a GPU reset while the host keeps sending the same SPS/PPS (VideoDecoder.swift:99-105).

ONE CMSampleBuffer PER FRAME, NOT PER SLICE. All picture NALs of the access unit are concatenated into one AVCC buffer and submitted as a single sample (VideoDecoder.swift:124-141, makeSampleBuffer at :320-374). So even if the new transport puts slices on the wire early, the current decoder API surface takes a whole frame. Changing to per-slice submission is a real code change, not a transport-only one.

TIMESTAMPS ARE FABRICATED LOCALLY. presentationTimeStamp = CACurrentMediaTime() at submit time, timescale 90000; duration and DTS are `.invalid` (VideoDecoder.swift:350-354). No host timestamp travels the wire today and nothing consumes one. Decode flags are `_EnableAsynchronousDecompression` + `_EnableTemporalProcessing` (VideoDecoder.swift:138).

DECODE OUTPUT. kCVPixelFormatType_32BGRA, Metal-compatible (VideoDecoder.swift:267-270). Hardware decode is required via kVTVideoDecoderSpecification_EnableHardwareAcceleratedVideoDecoder (VideoDecoder.swift:296-299).

ERROR RECOVERY THE TRANSPORT CAN TRIGGER. kVTInvalidSessionErr, kVTVideoDecoderMalfunctionErr and kVTVideoDecoderBadDataErr all invalidate the session and fire onKeyframeNeeded (VideoDecoder.swift:219-227); everything else logs and drops the frame, throttled to one line per 5 s (VideoDecoder.swift:209-217).

FRAME → WINDOW. Decoder callback runs on a VideoToolbox thread and fans one CVPixelBuffer out to every attached MetalView (StreamSession.swift:105-116) — ONE decode serves N windows, each blitting a different sub-rect, which is the whole reason multi-window is affordable (StreamSession.swift:8-15). MetalView.displayFrame is thread-safe and keeps only the NEWEST pending buffer, dropping the rest, then presents on the main thread (MetalView.swift:33-40, 136-156). Presentation is a Metal blit of `sourceRect` from a CVMetalTextureCache texture into the drawable, with the layer at bgra8Unorm, `.resizeAspect` gravity and an explicitly sRGB colorspace (MetalView.swift:55-71, 158-202).

AUDIO PATH. Datagram → strip 12-byte RTP header, check payload type 97 (drop 127 = parity), check sequence continuity and reset the decoder on a gap (StreamSession.swift:279-304) → AudioToolbox AudioConverter Opus→S16LE 48 kHz stereo, output buffer sized for the largest legal Opus frame, 5760 samples = 120 ms (OpusDecoder.swift:16-18, 73-106) → AudioRingBuffer, 500 ms capacity, 50 ms target, 120 ms ceiling, trimmed continuously in whole stereo frames so drift cannot ratchet into permanent latency (AudioRenderer.swift:196-308) → RemoteIO render callback.

COPIES PER FRAME, TODAY. recvfrom into a stack [UInt8] then copied into a Data (UdpStream.swift:159, 192); each shard copied again into the block dictionary (VideoDepacketizer.swift:206); all shards concatenated into a new Data (VideoDepacketizer.swift:215-219); trailing zeros trimmed one byte at a time in a loop (VideoDepacketizer.swift:254-257); then copied into a CMBlockBuffer (VideoDecoder.swift:323-344). At least four full copies of every frame before it reaches the decoder. A new transport is the natural place to remove most of them.

A CORRECTNESS FOOTGUN THE NEW TRANSPORT SHOULD NOT INHERIT: VideoDepacketizer trims ALL trailing zero bytes from the reassembled frame to undo FEC block padding (VideoDepacketizer.swift:253-257). That will also eat legitimate trailing zero bytes of the last NAL. With no FEC and explicit lengths this disappears.
survey.ports:
PORT ALLOCATIONS AND WHERE THEY ARE DEFINED.

CANONICAL WINDOWS DEFINITION — /Users/you/Desktop/SolStream/windows/SolStreamAgent/ports.h:
- kDefaultSunshineBase = 47600 (ports.h:38). Chosen so the derived block 47595–47621 is clear of Sunshine's default 47984–48010 and of 47989, so `netstat` on a dual-install machine shows two distinct groups (ports.h:35-37).
- kDefaultAgentPort = 47630 (ports.h:44). Deliberately OUTSIDE the derived block; it moved off 47997 because that sat inside Sunshine's default range (ports.h:41-43).
- enum class SunshinePort offsets (ports.h:47-55): kHttps = -5, kHttp = 0, kWebUi = +1, kVideo = +9, kControl = +10, kAudio = +11, kRtsp = +21.
- constexpr MapPort(base, which) (ports.h:57-59).

CANONICAL MAC DEFINITION — /Users/you/Desktop/SolStream/macos/SolStreamClient/Sources/StreamConnection/StreamPorts.swift:
- `.solstream` = base 47600 (StreamPorts.swift:21); `.sunshineDefault` = base 47989 (StreamPorts.swift:23).
- https = base-5 (:31), http = base (:33), webUI = base+1 (:36), video = base+9 (:37), control = base+10 (:38), audio = base+11 (:39), rtsp = base+21 (:40).
- `static let agent: UInt16 = 47630` (StreamPorts.swift:46) — fixed, not derived.
- `candidates = [.solstream, .sunshineDefault]` (StreamPorts.swift:54) so the client can also talk to a stock Sunshine.
Both files carry an explicit note that they mirror each other and must agree (ports.h:24-27, StreamPorts.swift:5-10).

RESOLVED NUMBERS AT THE 47600 BASE: https 47595, http 47600, web UI 47601, video 47609/UDP, control 47610/UDP, audio 47611/UDP, rtsp 47621, agent 47630/TCP.

FIREWALL RULES — /Users/you/Desktop/SolStream/windows/SolStreamAgent/installer.cpp:747-753, program-scoped and port-scoped:
- "SolStream - agent": SolStream.exe, TCP, kDefaultAgentPort (47630).
- "SolStream - Sunshine TCP": sunshine.exe, TCP, PortList{kHttps, kHttp, kRtsp} = 47595,47600,47621.
- "SolStream - Sunshine UDP": sunshine.exe, UDP, PortList{kVideo, kControl, kAudio} = 47609,47610,47611.
The web UI (47601) is deliberately NOT opened here — a program-only rule would expose it and the comment says so explicitly (installer.cpp:262-269). Removal at installer.cpp:787-795 also deletes four legacy rule names.

DISCREPANCY WORTH KNOWING: the standalone /Users/you/Desktop/SolStream/scripts/install-solstream-firewall.bat:89-94 DOES open the web UI 47601/TCP, and opens the media ports as a range 47609-47611. Its header (lines 11-12, 29-39) documents the same table. The two scripts disagree on 47601.

ORPHANED PORT CONSTANTS NOT IN ports.h — /Users/you/Desktop/SolStream/windows/ClipboardMonitor/clipboard_input_protocol.h:17-18: kClipboardWSPort = 47991 (TCP) and kInputUDPPort = 47990 (UDP). Both sit INSIDE Sunshine's default 47984–48010 block. ClipboardMonitor is built (CMakeLists.txt:164) and starts an InputReceiver on 47990 (ClipboardMonitor/main.cpp:165-175), but it does not ship (dist/SolStream contains only SolStream.exe, licenses/ and sunshine/) and the clipboard is handled inside the agent instead (main.cpp:1008). Note also that udp_input.cpp:91 assigns `INADDR_LOOPBACK` directly to `sin_addr.s_addr` without htonl, so that bind address is not what the comment says it is.

LOCAL PORTS THE MAC BINDS. Video and audio sockets try the SERVER's port number as a local bind hint and fall back to ephemeral (UdpStream.swift:71-92; StreamConnection.swift:973, 986) — the hint is admitted to be meaningless because the host replies to whatever port the ping came from (UdpStream.swift:58-62). The ENet control socket is created with `enet_host_create(nil, …)` so it takes an ephemeral port (ControlStream.swift:158).

MDNS. The Mac browses `_nvstream._tcp` (HostBrowser.swift:52), which Sunshine advertises itself; SolStream publishes nothing of its own. That produces duplicate rows on a machine with two Sunshines, worked around at HostBrowser.swift:143-207. A new transport gets no service record for free.
constraints: SINGLE AGENT CLIENT, SINGLE SESSION. The agent serves exactly one Mac; a second connection is refused with a {"type":"busy"} line rather than left in the accept backlog, and this only works because serving moved to its own thread (main.cpp:3951-4021, the reasoning at :3959-3977). Commands are handled one at a time on one thread per client (HandleCommand, main.cpp:2740). `launch` BLOCKS that thread until a window appears, up to 60 s (main.cpp:2932-2939). Any new transport must not need the agent thread to be responsive during a launch.

AGENT WRITES ARE SERIALISED BY ONE CRITICAL SECTION. g_send_cs guards every write to the client socket — command replies (main.cpp:3072-3088), cursor pushes, watcher pushes (main.cpp:1472, 1531, 1822-1848). A line torn in half by another thread is an unrecoverable desync because there are no request ids (main.cpp:3069-3071). Key material or session setup added to this channel inherits that serialisation.

THE AGENT CHANNEL IS PLAINTEXT AND SAYS SO. main.cpp:1239-1242: token auth 'does not encrypt the session or protect against someone who can read the traffic'. If media keys are derived from the agent session, the derivation input must not be something an observer of that TCP stream can read — the token itself is visible on the wire in the `auth` line today (AgentConnection.swift:387-396).

THE CANVAS IS FIXED FOR THE LIFE OF A SESSION. main.swift:562-566 states it outright: mode is negotiated at /launch and ANNOUNCE, so changing it later means tearing the session down. A Mac window resize is therefore a HOST-WINDOW resize inside a fixed canvas, driven over the agent channel by `place`, self-clocked to the round trip with at most one request queued (AppWindow.swift:403-427), during the drag rather than after it (AppWindow.swift:375-384). Renegotiation as a transport feature is a NEW capability, not a port of an existing one.

CANVAS SIZE IS CLAMPED TO 4096 ON BOTH AXES for NVENC H.264 — above it the handshake succeeds and no frame ever arrives, and a 16-inch MacBook Pro at More Space asks for 4112x2658, so this is reachable with ordinary hardware (main.swift:420-422, 567-577).

THE HOST CAN ONLY SWITCH BETWEEN MODES THE DISPLAY DRIVER ALREADY ENUMERATES. Adding a mode needs a device restart, so the ladder is seeded once at setup (main.cpp:410-415). A requested canvas may not be achievable and the reply says what was achieved (main.cpp:2872-2884).

MEDIA SOCKETS FILTER ON SOURCE ADDRESS AND PORT IN USERSPACE. UdpStream.drain rejects any datagram not from the exact serverAddr ip+port and counts the rejects (UdpStream.swift:181-207). This is a deliberate anti-injection measure — one crafted packet can wedge the depacketizer into waiting for a frame that never completes. But it also means a HOST-side address change mid-session breaks reception silently. NAT rebinding survival has to come from an authenticated in-band signal, not from trusting a new source address.

CONTROL-PATH LATENCY IS QUANTISED TO 50 ms TODAY. ControlStream's service loop calls enet_host_service(host, &event, 50) and only then drains queued input and pending IDR requests (ControlStream.swift:221-285). sendInput merely appends to an array under a lock (ControlStream.swift:135-139). So on an idle control channel an input event can wait up to a full 50 ms before it is even encrypted. On a 0.5–2 ms LAN that is 25–100× the network cost. This is the single largest avoidable input latency in the current design.

THE CONTROL THREAD IS OCCUPIED FOR THE WHOLE SESSION. 'anything queued behind the loop would not run until the loop exits' — so cross-thread state is passed by a plain NSLock, not by dispatching onto the queue (ControlStream.swift:49-58).

THREE QUEUES, DELIBERATELY SEPARATE. com.solstream.connection (userInitiated), com.solstream.video (userInteractive), com.solstream.audio (userInitiated) — 'so audio handling can never delay video depacketization, and so their ping timers don't fire in lockstep' (StreamConnection.swift:106-110). Video ingest, depacketizing, decode submission and the stats timer all run on the video queue.

STREAM OBJECT LIFETIME IS A REAL HAZARD, ALREADY PAID FOR. The three stream references are guarded by streamLock and accessors retain before unlocking, because an unsynchronised read is a use-after-free rather than a stale read (StreamConnection.swift:131-165). quiesceMedia() exists specifically to make socket callbacks quiescent before the Opus decoder and audio renderer are released (StreamConnection.swift:249-274, StreamSession.swift:238-255). VideoDecoder takes an NSLock around decode/shutdown for the same reason (VideoDecoder.swift:37-42).

PRESENTATION IS NEWEST-WINS AND MUST STAY THAT WAY. Queueing a block per frame would build an unbounded backlog and stall the UI; only the newest pixel buffer is kept (MetalView.swift:33-40, 136-156).

SO_RCVBUF IS 2 MB ON EACH MEDIA SOCKET, sized for 'a couple of frames' worth of packets' so a scheduling hiccup does not become dropped video (UdpStream.swift:83-85). One readiness notification is drained in a loop until EWOULDBLOCK (UdpStream.swift:157-193).

NO FEC RECOVERY EXISTS ALREADY — parity shards are received, counted and discarded, and loss is answered with an IDR request (VideoDepacketizer.swift:36-38, 139-142). The IDR request is rate-limited to 2/s because unthrottled requests turned loss into a bandwidth spike that caused more loss (ControlStream.swift:99-120). Any LTR/intra-refresh scheme must keep an equivalent damper.

THE MAC HAS NO REMOTE SWIFTPM DEPENDENCIES BUT DOES VENDOR C. Package.swift:14 is `dependencies: []`, but Sources/CEnet is a vendored ENet C library (8 .c files plus headers, MIT LICENSE present) built as a local target (Package.swift:97-106) and Sources/CCommonCrypto is a bridging module. Replacing ENet is what would make the Mac client genuinely dependency-free in the media path.
OPUS ON THE MAC IS ALREADY DEPENDENCY-FREE. It uses AudioToolbox's kAudioFormatOpus via AudioConverter, not libopus (OpusDecoder.swift:1-9, 34-64). libopus is therefore only a Windows-side concern.

BCRYPT AES-256-GCM IS ALREADY LINKED AND ALREADY WRITTEN. The agent links bcrypt (SolStreamAgent/CMakeLists.txt:65) and uses BCryptGenRandom (main.cpp:1259). A complete working BCrypt AES-GCM open/decrypt with cached BCRYPT_ALG_HANDLE/BCRYPT_KEY_HANDLE, plus a sliding replay window, already exists at windows/ClipboardMonitor/udp_input.cpp:140-273 with constants at clipboard_input_protocol.h:119-122 (32-byte key, 12-byte nonce, 16-byte tag, 1024-slot replay window). It is a usable reference — but note its nonce is sent on the wire in full (udp_input.cpp:192-213) rather than derived, and its replay bitmap is a single uint64 compared against a window size of 1024 (udp_input.h:49, udp_input.cpp:24-53), which is inconsistent.

THE MAC ALREADY DOES DETERMINISTIC 96-BIT GCM NONCES. ControlStream.encode builds a 12-byte IV as a little-endian uint32 sequence in bytes 0-3 with a two-byte direction/stream tag at [10],[11] — 'CC' outbound, 'HC' inbound — explicitly citing NIST SP 800-38D 8.2.1 (ControlStream.swift:315-320, 412-421). That is the shape of construction the new transport needs, but its counter is a bare uint32 that wraps with no rekey (ControlStream.swift:409-410) and is not bound to any session id, so it repeats across reconnects that reuse a key.

SHIPPED SURFACE IS SMALLER THAN THE REPO. dist/SolStream contains SolStream.exe (the agent), licenses/ and sunshine/. windows/sunshine is explicitly NOT built (CMakeLists.txt:161-163 and windows/sunshine/README.md), CaptureHelper, ClipboardMonitor, InputInjector and FileTransferService build but do not ship. Sunshine is shipped UNMODIFIED on purpose because it is GPL-3.0 and modifying it changes the licence position (windows/sunshine/README.md).

THE ONE THING CONFIGURATION CANNOT BUY IS SUB-RECTANGLE ENCODING. Sunshine encodes the whole capture display, so a window smaller than the canvas spends bitrate and encoder time on pixels nobody sees; today the seeded mode ladder keeps the canvas close to the window to make the waste small (windows/sunshine/README.md). A SolStream-owned encoder path removes this constraint — and windows/CaptureHelper already implements per-HWND WinRT Graphics Capture into a D3D11 shared-texture ring with a named-pipe protocol (capture.h:56-59, pipe_transport.h:35-52), currently consumed by nothing.

AGENT-SIDE PUSH CADENCES THE NEW TRANSPORT MUST NOT COLLIDE WITH: cursor watcher 40 ms poll (main.cpp:3206, 3228), window watcher 120 ms poll (main.cpp:1962), Mac heartbeat every 10 s against a 30 s host idle timeout (AgentConnection.swift:198; main.cpp:3266, 3320-3323), Mac window-status poll and clipboard poll each 1.0 s (AppWindow.swift:139; ClipboardBridge.swift:42).
unknowns: NO MEASURED PACKET OR FRAME SIZES EXIST ANYWHERE IN THE TREE. There is no captured log, no benchmark, no recorded stats line with real numbers. Everything I have given for 1080p60 slice/frame size is arithmetic from the configured defaults (1920x1080, 60 fps, 20000 kbps at StreamConnection.swift:43-45), not observation. The memory note streaming-pipeline-status.md describes a [stats] line printed every 2 s during a live run against 100.101.102.103 but records no values from it. If real slice-size distributions matter to the design, they have to be measured — the note's own instruction is to run `./.build/debug/SolStreamClient --host <ip> --launch "File Explorer" --screenshot-after 30` and read the stats line.

OPUS PACKET SIZE IN BYTES IS NOT RECORDED. The 5 ms frame duration is negotiated (StreamConnection.swift:807) and the packet rate is stated as ~200/s (StreamSession.swift:242-243), but no code or comment states the byte size of a typical packet, and the audio bitrate is never configured by SolStream — it is Sunshine's default, which this tree does not set (sunshine_host.cpp:550-591 writes no audio or bitrate keys at all).

MOUSE-MOVE EVENT RATE IS NOT MEASURED. InputCapture counts mouseMovedSeen and positionsSent (InputCapture.swift:165-167) and the stats line prints them (StreamConnection.swift:1013), but no recorded value exists. There is no coalescing, so the rate is whatever AppKit delivers for the user's device.

THE 16-VERSUS-32 BYTE VIDEO HEADER CONTRADICTION IS UNRESOLVED IN THE SOURCE. StreamConnection.swift:34-35 says the datagram is packetSize plus a 16-byte header; VideoDepacketizer.swift:40 and ProtocolTests.swift:15 both use 32. I did not resolve which the host actually emits, because doing so would require reading the host's packetizer, which the clean-room rule forbids. Treat the derived 1040-byte datagram figure as coming from SolStream's own test model, not from an authority.

I DID NOT DETERMINE THE HOST'S IDR INTERVAL, ENCODER PRESET, SLICE COUNT, OR WHETHER LTR IS AVAILABLE ON THE ENCODERS IN USE. Nothing in SolStream's tree configures any of these — sunshine_host.cpp writes only port, origin_web_ui_allowed, output_name, capture=ddx, log/cred/state/apps paths, cert/pkey and system_tray (sunshine_host.cpp:550-591). Everything else is upstream default, and finding out would mean reading source that is off limits here.

NO WINDOWS-SIDE ENCODER EXISTS IN THIS TREE TO PUT SLICES ON THE WIRE FROM. windows/CaptureHelper produces D3D11 textures over a named pipe and is consumed by nothing; windows/sunshine (the intended consumer) is not built. Where the new transport's Windows sender lives, and what hands it encoded slices, is an open question this inventory cannot answer from the code.

HOW THE NEW TRANSPORT'S SESSION KEYS WOULD BE CARRIED IS NOT PRE-DECIDED BY ANYTHING EXISTING. The agent channel has no key-exchange command and no field reserved for one; kProtocolVersion is 1 (main.cpp:70) and there is no negotiation of capabilities beyond that single integer. Adding a command is straightforward, but nothing constrains its shape today.

NO IPv6 ANYWHERE IN THE MEDIA PATH. UdpStream is AF_INET only (UdpStream.swift:73, 96-103, 133-144) and the agent listener is AF_INET only with an IPv4-only --bind parser (main.cpp:3753, 3769-3775). HostBrowser can resolve an IPv6 address but skips link-local (HostBrowser.swift:115-118). Whether the new transport must be dual-stack is undecided by the code.

PATH MTU IS ASSUMED, NEVER DISCOVERED. The only MTU knowledge in the tree is the comment that Tailscale and WireGuard links are 1280 (StreamConnection.swift:35) and a --packet-size command-line override (main.swift:59-67). Nothing probes, and nothing reacts to an ICMP fragmentation-needed.

designs.name: SSMT — SolStream Media Transport v1
designs.oneLine: One AES-256-GCM-sealed UDP socket per direction pair with a 20-byte total per-datagram overhead, where a single 4-byte cleartext sequence number simultaneously serves as the GCM invocation field, the loss-detection sequence and the retransmit-ring index; video goes on the wire slice-by-slice as the encoder produces it, and loss is answered by a three-tier ladder — bounded retransmit, then LTR-referenced repair frame, then intra-refresh — with no FEC anywhere.
designs.strongest:
One 4-byte cleartext field does three jobs: it is the AES-GCM invocation field (so no nonce is transmitted), the loss-detection sequence for every packet type at once (so a lost keystroke, a lost Opus frame and a lost video fragment are all detected by the same check at the same instant), and the sender's retransmit-ring index (so repair lookup is `ring[seq & 255]`). That collapse is why total per-datagram overhead is 20 bytes with a 98.2% payload ratio at full MTU, and it is why there is no separate per-stream sequencing, no FEC block accounting, and no head-of-line blocking anywhere in the design.

The close second is what it makes affordable: because a shared sequence space detects loss within microseconds, and because a LAN RTT is 0.5–2 ms against a 16.7 ms frame period, a single lost fragment can be NACK'd and repaired *inside the same frame's assembly window* — with a hard deadline test on the sender that makes retransmission incapable of ever adding latency. That turns LTR from the first line of defence into the second, and reserves it for the losses that actually matter.
designs.weakest:
The token still travels the plaintext agent channel today, and the design's own fix for that is a protocol change both ends have to ship before the media handshake is genuinely authenticated. Until `auth` becomes challenge-response (v2), anyone who captured a single `auth` line — at any point in the past, on any network the Mac has used — holds the token, and the token is what binds the ECDH. Such an attacker can sit between the two, substitute their own P-256 key on each side, and compute both `bind` and `confirm`. The ECDH gives real forward secrecy against a *passive* observer immediately, which is a genuine improvement over deriving keys from the token directly; but against an active attacker the whole construction rests on a value that `main.cpp:1239-1242` correctly warns is not confidential. The v2 change is about twenty lines on each side and should land in the same commit as the transport, not after it. I would not ship the media path without it.

The second weak point is scope rather than security, and it is larger. This design presupposes a Windows-side encoder that emits slices as it produces them, exposes LTR slot marking and per-slot reference selection, and supports dynamic bitrate reconfigure and a switch into continuous intra-refresh. No such encoder exists in this tree. `windows/CaptureHelper` produces D3D11 textures over a named pipe and is consumed by nothing; `windows/sunshine` is not built and is shipped unmodified on purpose. I also could not verify from SolStream's own code whether the NVENC/AMF/QSV paths actually in use expose LTR — the survey lists that as an explicit unknown and finding out would have meant reading source that is off limits here. If LTR turns out to be unavailable on some encoder, Tier 2 collapses into Tier 3 and the design still works, but the repair cost goes from one P-frame to half a second of intra-refresh. The transport is the easy half of this work.

Third, smaller: every packet size in the design is arithmetic from configured defaults, because there is not one measured slice size, frame size or Opus packet size anywhere in the repository. The 256-entry retransmit ring, the reorder threshold of 8, and the four-deep input redundancy window are all reasoned rather than measured, and the first thing to do after the loopback conformance test is to run the stats line against a real host and check them.

designs.name: SMT/1 — SolStream Media Transport, version 1
designs.oneLine: One UDP socket carrying AES-256-GCM-sealed datagrams, keyed by an ephemeral P-256 exchange run over the existing authenticated agent JSON channel, with a per-direction ratcheted key schedule, a 48-bit counter nonce that cannot repeat by construction, no retransmission of anything, and loss recovery by client-confirmed long-term reference frames.
designs.strongest:
ltrHave: the client tells the host, sixty times a second, exactly which
long-term reference frames it is holding intact — an 8-bit bitmap in a packet it
is already sending.

Everything good about the recovery design falls out of that one field. The host
never has to infer from a loss report which old frame the client might still
have; it looks up a bitmap and picks the newest confirmed slot. Recovery becomes
a single P-sized frame at one round trip, instead of an IDR at five to ten times
the bytes behind a 500 ms damper that exists only because IDR storms made loss
worse. It turns the FEC question inside out: the reason you do not need parity
is not that you can reconstruct the lost packet, it is that you already know a
frame both ends agree on and can just predict from that instead. And it makes
the host's LTR marking policy safe to be aggressive, because a slot the client
never confirms is simply never used — a marked-but-unconfirmed slot costs
nothing and risks nothing.

The second-order effect is what makes it worth the field: because recovery is
cheap, the damper on it can be 33 ms instead of 500 ms, which means the client
can afford to report damage the instant it detects it rather than batching, which
means detection latency collapses to one frame period. The expensive-recovery
design forced conservative reporting; the cheap-recovery design permits eager
reporting, and eager reporting is what actually shortens the visible glitch.
designs.weakest:
The LTR loop — the best part of this design — depends on encoder capabilities
that nothing in this tree has verified, and it has no fallback that preserves its
headline number.

It assumes the Windows encoder can (a) mark an arbitrary frame into a chosen
long-term reference slot, (b) force the next frame to predict from a chosen slot
on demand, mid-stream, (c) run a rolling intra-refresh wave and turn it on and
off, and (d) emit slice-level output as slices complete rather than at end of
frame. NVENC exposes all four; AMF and Quick Sync expose subsets, and the exact
subset varies by driver. The survey is explicit that nothing in SolStream
configures the encoder at all — sunshine_host.cpp:550-591 writes no encoder keys
— so I have no evidence about which encoder will actually be under this, how many
LTR slots it offers, or whether per-frame reference control is available without
a reconfigure. If it turns out to be two slots with no per-frame control, the
LTR window shrinks to ~260 ms, recovery falls back to intra-refresh plus IDR,
and the 33 ms recovery figure evaporates. The design degrades gracefully in
correctness terms and badly in the terms it was sold on.

The second weakness is that every quantitative claim here is arithmetic, not
measurement. The tree contains no captured packet sizes, no slice-size
distribution, no Opus packet size, no mouse-event rate, no IDR interval. Fragment
counts, the 64-frame damagedMask window, the 8-frame LTR marking cadence, the
16 ms feedback period and the priority scheduler's worst-case delays are all
derived from configured defaults and from what the link ought to do. The first
real capture could move any of them. The header fields are sized with enough
slack that they should survive being wrong; the cadences will need retuning.

Third, and separable: the security of all of this still rests on a 128-bit
bearer token sitting in a plaintext file on Windows and in an unprotected
UserDefaults plist on the Mac. The key schedule limits the blast radius — a
token stolen tomorrow does not decrypt what was recorded today — but it does not
change the fact that the strongest link in the chain is anchored to the weakest
one, and that moving the token into the Keychain and DPAPI is worth more than
any refinement to this protocol.

synthesis.name: SMT/1 — SolStream Media Transport, version 1
synthesis.rationale:
SPINE: design 2 (SMT/1). GRAFTS: design 1 (SSMT). Note: only two designs were supplied, not three.

Design 2 wins the spine on the thing that must not be wrong. Its nonce is a secret 6-byte fixed field concatenated with a 48-bit counter carried verbatim on the wire: nothing reconstructed, nothing truncated. Design 1 packs the epoch into the top two bits of a 32-bit wire field, making the wire value a truncation rather than the invocation field itself. That is provably fine and it is exactly the subtlety that kills you where a bug is silent. Four extra bytes per datagram is 0.28% at a 1500 MTU.

Design 2 also brings per-direction keys as disjoint ranges of one HKDF-Expand output plus a chain ratchet with zeroisation (intra-session forward secrecy; direction confusion impossible rather than unlikely); ltrHave, the best single idea in either document; path-validation before migrating the send target; a persisted hcount so a host with a broken RNG still derives distinct keys; and an honestly enumerated threat model.

Design 1 supplies what design 2 got wrong by being too pure: bounded tier-1 retransmission with a sender-side deadline test, byte-offset fragmentation, microsecond capture timestamps, the DISCARDABLE bit, inline parameter sets ahead of every IDR, and the never-overwrite-the-acked-LTR-slot invariant.

WHAT NEITHER DESIGN KNOWS. /Users/you/Desktop/SolStream/spike/wgc-capture/RESULTS.md (run today) proves per-window WGC capture works borderless from an unpackaged binary, survives full occlusion with an unchanged latency distribution, and is CHANGE-DRIVEN: 241 frames for 240 paints, and a still window costs nothing. Both designs assume video arrives continuously. It does not. Four consequences, all mine:

1. A new packet type 0x13 HOSTBEAT, every 100 ms whenever no VIDEO went out, carrying ENCODER_IDLE and lastFrameId. Without it the Mac cannot distinguish a static window from a dead host, and StreamSession.swift's "1 s of no frames = stream lost" watchdog becomes actively wrong.
2. Loss detection cannot rest on the counter-threshold rule alone; the timeout rule and the 25 ms frame-closure timer become load-bearing rather than belt-and-braces.
3. The LTR marking cadence is in FRAMES, not milliseconds. A wall-clock cadence over a static window marks nothing, then marks a burst.
4. Bitrate control is gated on ENCODER_IDLE == 0. Goodput measured across a static window is meaningless and would drive the controller to the floor.

Also mine: psGen in the video header, so a frame cannot be decoded under stale parameter sets after a renegotiation.

The transport is the easy half. The encoder that emits slices with LTR control does not exist in this tree, and the build order is arranged so that unknown is measured at step 6 rather than assumed at step 1.

OUTER HEADER — 8 BYTES CLEARTEXT ON EVERY DATAGRAM, NO EXCEPTIONS.

  off  w  field
   0   1  verEpoch   high nibble = version (1); low nibble = key epoch mod 16
   1   1  sessTag    low byte of the derived 32-bit session id
   2   6  counter    48-bit BIG-ENDIAN, per-direction AEAD invocation number
   8   N  ciphertext N = datagramLen - 24
 8+N  16  tag        AES-256-GCM authentication tag

AAD = the 8 cleartext bytes verbatim.
Nonce = F(direction, epoch) [6 bytes, secret, never transmitted] || counter [6 bytes, copied verbatim from bytes 2..7].

TAG AT THE END, not before the ciphertext (design 1 put it before). The sender builds one buffer, writes plaintext at offset 8, and calls BCryptEncrypt with pbInput = buf+8, pbOutput = buf+8 (in place) and authInfo.pbTag = buf+8+N. One buffer, no assembly step, and the ciphertext starts 8-byte aligned instead of design 1's offset 20. The receiver does recvfrom into a pooled buffer and decrypts in place, so plaintext lands at offset 8 and the inner header parses where the ciphertext was.

ALL INNER OFFSETS BELOW ARE PLAINTEXT-RELATIVE. Absolute datagram offset = plaintext offset + 8.

Everything except those 8 bytes is encrypted, including the packet type. There is no cleartext type field and no cleartext length field. The datagram length is the length.

sessTag is 8 bits of a truncated secret, so it is not a stable cross-session identifier an observer can correlate on. Its jobs are O(1) demux across the brief window where an old and a new session coexist during reconnect, and rejecting 255/256 of a forged flood with a byte compare instead of an AES-GCM verify — a real 256x DoS cost reduction. The tag is always the authority; sessTag is never trusted for anything.

Byte order is BIG-ENDIAN throughout, with no exceptions. InputProtocol.swift:15 documents a little-endian keycode inside an otherwise big-endian packet and calls the asymmetry deliberate; it is not carried over.

FIXED OVERHEAD: 24 bytes (8 header + 16 tag) plus the per-type inner header.
Video: 24 + 16 = 40. At a 1500 MTU that leaves 1432 bytes of coded video in a 1472-byte UDP payload — 97.3% payload efficiency, with no FEC parity being paid for and discarded as VideoDepacketizer.swift:139-142 does today.

CLEAN-ROOM NOTE. I read no Sunshine, Moonlight or moonlight-common-c source. SolStream's own files that I read (VideoDepacketizer.swift, InputProtocol.swift, ControlStream.swift) contain comments describing GameStream layouts; I used those only to learn what the current code expects to be handed. SMT/1 shares no field, offset, width, magic or constant with what those comments describe. Twice I caught myself reaching for "the shape the old one had" — a 32-byte video header and a 12-byte RTP prefix on audio — and discarded both, sizing from the requirement instead.
synthesis.packetTypes:
Nine types. The type byte is the first plaintext byte, so it is encrypted. An unrecognised type means "peer is newer" and is ignored silently.

  0x01 PING      both       0x02 PONG      both
  0x03 SESSION   both       0x10 VIDEO     host->Mac
  0x11 AUDIO     host->Mac  0x12 PARAMSETS host->Mac
  0x13 HOSTBEAT  host->Mac  0x20 INPUT     Mac->host
  0x21 FEEDBACK  Mac->host

=== 0x10 VIDEO, 16-byte inner header ===
  +0   1  type = 0x10
  +1   1  flags  b0 FRAME_START  b1 SLICE_END  b2 FRAME_END  b3 IDR
                 b4 PARAMSETS_INLINE  b5 INTRA_REFRESH  b6 RECOVERY_POINT
                 b7 DISCARDABLE (nothing will reference this frame)
  +2   1  ltr    mark:4 (high) | ref:4 (low). 0xF = not marked / predicts from
                 the immediately previous frame. ref is 0xF on an IDR.
  +3   1  sliceId  0..254 within the frame; 255 reserved
  +4   4  frameId  u32 BE. At 60 fps a u32 lasts 2.2 years: no wrap arithmetic
                   anywhere in the receiver.
  +8   3  fragOff  u24 BE, byte offset of this fragment within the frame's AVCC
                   byte stream. NOT a fragment index.
  +11  1  psGen    parameter-set generation this frame decodes under
  +12  4  captureUs u32 BE, host monotonic microseconds at capture
  +16  .. slice bytes, AVCC form

FIXED, not conditional. Design 1 made 8 of these bytes present only on the first fragment; that saves ~224 bytes on a ~42 KB frame (0.5%) and buys a differently-parsed header on the path carrying 97% of the bytes.

fragOff, not a fragment index, because the sender flushes at every slice boundary so fragments are variable-length and an index does not tell the receiver where to put the bytes. A byte offset makes reassembly a memcpy at base+fragOff. FRAME_END gives totalLen = fragOff + payloadLen. 3 bytes covers 16 MB per frame.

No sliceCount and no fragCount: at the moment slice 0's first fragment leaves the encoder neither is knowable, which is the whole point of slice-early transmission. End flags carry the structure; the counts fall out of the fragment that carries the flag.

psGen is mine. Without it a frame encoded before a renegotiation can be decoded under the parameter sets that replaced it. One byte, one race gone.

PAYLOAD IS AVCC, NOT ANNEX-B: each NAL prefixed with its own u32 BE length, exactly what VideoDecoder.swift:124-128 builds by hand today. The host must scan the encoder's Annex-B output for slice boundaries to packetize at all, so the conversion is free there and it deletes the Mac's start-code scan (VideoDecoder.swift:162-194). AUD, SEI and filler are dropped host-side rather than sent and discarded (VideoDecoder.swift:85-97). Picture data never contains SPS/PPS except when PARAMSETS_INLINE says it does.

=== 0x11 AUDIO, 12-byte inner header ===
  +0   1  type = 0x11
  +1   1  flags  b0 DISCONTINUITY (first frame after an encoder reset)
                 b1 HAS_PREV (frame audioSeq-1 is appended)
  +2   2  audioSeq u16 BE, of the CURRENT frame
  +4   4  captureUs u32 BE
  +8   2  curLen   u16 BE, length of the current Opus frame
  +10  2  reserved (0)
  +12  .. current Opus frame, curLen bytes
       .. previous Opus frame if HAS_PREV; length = plaintextLen - 12 - curLen

One 5 ms Opus frame per datagram. HAS_PREV arms when measured loss exceeds 0.2%: a single-packet loss becomes inaudible instead of a 5 ms hole, a two-packet burst becomes a 5 ms hole instead of 10 ms. This is redundant transmission, not FEC — no parity, no erasure code, nothing to reconstruct.

Honest: overhead is 24+12 = 36 bytes on a ~60-byte Opus frame, about 37% of the audio stream and about 0.25% of the link. Bundling two frames per datagram would halve it and cost 5 ms. Not taken.

=== 0x12 PARAMSETS, 12-byte inner header ===
  +0  1 type=0x12   +1  1 psGen   +2  1 codec (1=H.264 2=HEVC 3=AV1)
  +3  1 nalLen (NAL length prefix size in the video stream; always 4 in v1)
  +4  2 width u16 BE   +6 2 height u16 BE   +8 1 setCount   +9 3 reserved
  +12 .. setCount x [ u16 BE length ][ NAL bytes ]

Sent at session start, on every change, and every 200 ms until FEEDBACK reports psGenHave == psGen. This answers the one hard ordering requirement in the video path: the decoder cannot build a format description without SPS+PPS and re-asks for an IDR every 0.5 s until it has them (VideoDecoder.swift:103-120). Belt and braces from design 1: SPS/PPS are ALSO inlined ahead of every IDR's first slice (PARAMSETS_INLINE), ~60 bytes per IDR, making the ordering unconditional.

=== 0x13 HOSTBEAT, 24 bytes === (MINE — the WGC consequence)
  +0   1  type = 0x13
  +1   1  hostFlags b0 ENCODER_IDLE (WGC has delivered nothing; screen static)
                    b1 ENCODER_PAUSED  b2 DEGRADED (intra-refresh running)
                    b3 LTR_UNAVAILABLE (tier 2 disabled)  b4 CAPTURE_LOST
  +2   2  inputMiss  u16 BE, first missing input evSeq; 0xFFFF = none
  +4   4  inputAck   u32 BE, all events with evSeq <= this are applied
  +8   4  hostUs     u32 BE, host monotonic microseconds now
  +12  4  lastFrameId u32 BE, newest frame the host has emitted
  +16  4  bitrateKbps u32 BE, what the encoder is configured at now
  +20  1  psGen      +21 3 reserved

Sent every 100 ms whenever no VIDEO datagram went out in the last 100 ms, and immediately when inputAck advances. ENCODER_IDLE + lastFrameId is what lets the Mac tell "nothing changed" from "host died" — the distinction WGC's change-driven delivery destroys. inputMiss lets the Mac resend one specific event at once rather than waiting for its redundancy window to cover it.

=== 0x20 INPUT, 16-byte inner header ===
  +0   1  type = 0x20
  +1   1  count      0..15 events in this datagram
  +2   2  stateFlags u16 BE, AUTHORITATIVE bitmap of what the Mac believes is
            held: b0 shift b1 ctrl b2 alt b3 meta, b4..b8 mouse buttons 1..5
  +4   2  posX  u16 BE, absolute pointer X in canvas pixels; 0xFFFF = none
  +6   2  posY  u16 BE
  +8   2  refW  u16 BE, reference rectangle these coordinates are in
  +10  2  refH  u16 BE
  +12  4  baseSeq u32 BE, evSeq of the FIRST event carried; consecutive from there
  +16  .. count x [ u8 evType ][ u8 evLen ][ evLen bytes body ]

  0x01 KEY_DOWN 4 {u16 BE vk, u8 mods, u8 flags}   0x02 KEY_UP 4 {same}
  0x03 BUTTON_DOWN 1 {u8 button 1=L 2=M 3=R 4/5=extra}  0x04 BUTTON_UP 1
  0x05 SCROLL_V 2 {i16 BE, Windows clicks x120}    0x06 SCROLL_H 2 {i16 BE}
  0x07 KEY_RESET 0 (release everything held)       0x08 TEXT n (UTF-8, IME)
  0x09 REL_MOVE 4 {i16 BE dx, i16 BE dy}

THERE IS NO MOUSE_MOVE EVENT TYPE. Every INPUT datagram IS a position update, applied by the host BEFORE the events it carries. That makes "a button-down is always preceded by its position" (InputCapture.swift:391-402) a property of a single datagram, so packet loss cannot break it. A pure mouse move is count = 0.

Two classes in one packet: position is STATE (newest wins, never retransmitted, ordered by the transport counter alone); keys, buttons, scroll and relative motion are EVENTS (each with its own evSeq, applied exactly once in order).

ORDER-CRITICAL EVENTS SURVIVE LOSS BY REDUNDANCY, NOT RETRANSMISSION. Each datagram repeats the last R key/button events as well as the new one; R = 3 normally, up to 7 when loss exceeds 0.5%. Seven repeats of a ~6-byte event costs 42 bytes and survives seven consecutive losses with ZERO added latency and zero ARQ state. An ARQ would cost a round trip on the one class of traffic where a round trip is unaffordable.

evSeq is u32, not design 1's u16: a u16 wraps in about a minute of scrolling and forces wrap arithmetic into the host's dedup path.

If a gap in baseSeq persists 30 ms the host sets inputMiss; if it persists 100 ms it declares desync and the Mac sends KEY_RESET followed by the true state. Combined with stateFlags on every datagram, a lost key-up self-heals at the next input packet instead of becoming a stuck key — which is what InputCapture.swift:329-350's compensating machinery exists to paper over today.

=== 0x21 FEEDBACK, 52 bytes fixed + 7 per NACK range ===
  +0  1 type=0x21
  +1  1 flags b0 REQUEST_IDR  b1 REQUEST_LTR_RECOVERY  b2 DECODER_STALLED
              b3 PARAMSETS_MISSING  b4 WINDOW_HIDDEN (occluded: pause encoding)
  +2  2 reportSeq u16 BE
  +4  4 lastGoodFrame u32 BE     highest frameId complete AND decoded
  +8  4 highestFrameSeen u32 BE
  +12 8 damagedMask u64 BE       bit n = frame (highestFrameSeen-1-n) damaged
  +20 6 rxCounter u48 BE         highest transport counter accepted
  +26 1 psGenHave    +27 1 ltrHave (bitmap of LTR slots held INTACT)
  +28 4 rxPackets u32 BE   +32 4 rxBytes u32 BE   (since previous report)
  +36 4 lostPackets u32 BE +40 4 jitterUs u32 BE
  +44 4 frameAgeUs u32 BE        capture -> presented, from captureUs
  +48 1 ltrGen  +49 1 nackCount (0..8)  +50 2 reserved
  +52 .. nackCount x [ u48 BE startCounter ][ u8 run ]

Every 16 ms, plus immediately on declared loss with a 4 ms floor. NACKs are in TRANSPORT COUNTER space because the sender's retransmit ring is indexed by counter — the receiver never needs to know which frame a lost datagram belonged to. rxPackets/rxBytes/lostPackets are exactly the counters that already exist unused at UdpStream.swift:31-36 and VideoDepacketizer.swift:76-88; the lossStats type at ControlStream.swift:23 is declared and never constructed anywhere.

=== 0x01 PING / 0x02 PONG ===
  PING  +0 1 type=0x01  +1 1 flags (b0 MTU_PROBE b1 PATH_CHALLENGE b2 KEEPALIVE)
        +2 2 pingId u16 BE  +4 8 txUs u64 BE  +12 8 challenge u64 BE
        +20 .. zero padding to the probe size (MTU_PROBE only)
  PONG  +0 1 type=0x02  +1 1 flags (echoed)  +2 2 pingId  +4 8 txUs (verbatim)
        +12 8 challenge (verbatim)  +20 4 rxSizeBytes u32 BE  +24 4 turnaroundUs

RTT = now - txUs - turnaroundUs, so the responder's scheduling delay does not inflate the estimate. Mac pings every 200 ms (keepalive + RTT + NAT binding refresh). The host pings only to probe MTU and to validate a path, because it is the one sending large packets. Nothing in the tree measures RTT today — the UI number is ENet's own estimate (ControlStream.swift:64-73), which disappears with ENet.

=== 0x03 SESSION ===
  +0 1 type=0x03  +1 1 op  +2 2 seq u16 BE  +4 2 ackSeq u16 BE  +6 2 reserved
  +8 .. body
  op: 1 START  2 START_ACK  3 RENEGOTIATE  4 RENEG_ACK  5 STOP  6 STOP_ACK
  RENEGOTIATE body (12): u16 w, u16 h, u16 fps, u32 bitrateKbps, u8 codec, u8 flags
  RENEG_ACK body (8):    u16 w, u16 h, u16 fps, u8 psGen, u8 result
  STOP body (1): u8 reason

Reliable by repetition, never by ARQ: retransmit every 20 ms until the peer's ackSeq covers it, 50 attempts, then declare the session failed. Tiny, so repetition is free and it can never queue behind or block anything.

HOW THEY SHARE THE WIRE. One UDP socket, one port, both directions. Host binds 47631/UDP — adjacent to the agent's 47630/TCP and outside Sunshine's derived 47595-47621 block. Add kDefaultMediaPort = 47631 to /Users/you/Desktop/SolStream/windows/SolStreamAgent/ports.h next to kDefaultAgentPort, and StreamPorts.media = 47631 to StreamPorts.swift; both files already carry the note that they mirror each other and must agree. Firewall: one program-scoped rule "SolStream - media", SolStream.exe, UDP 47631, added to BOTH installer.cpp:747-753 and scripts/install-solstream-firewall.bat:89-94 — those two already disagree about 47601 and adding it to one would widen the disagreement.

One socket rather than three is a decision. Three means three bindings that migrate independently, three replay windows, three counters and three nonce-uniqueness arguments. The tree already carries the scar: two media sockets sharing one host-side endpoint out-param made video arrive on the audio port, and the fix was to stagger ping timers by 250 ms (UdpStream.swift:62-70). With one socket that race cannot be constructed.

NO HEAD-OF-LINE BLOCKING BY CONSTRUCTION. There is no ordering guarantee and no reliability layer, so nothing can wait behind a retransmission. The only shared serialising resource is the send queue, scheduled by strict priority at DATAGRAM granularity:
  host->Mac: AUDIO > PARAMSETS/SESSION/PONG/HOSTBEAT > VIDEO-retransmit > VIDEO
  Mac->host: INPUT > FEEDBACK/SESSION/PING
Worst case an audio frame waits one datagram serialisation behind a video fragment: ~12 us at 1 Gbps, ~1.2 ms at 10 Mbps. Video never holds the scheduler for more than one datagram, so audio cannot be starved.

RECEIVE SIDE: one reader thread does recvfrom, AEAD open and demux ONLY, handing plaintext to the existing com.solstream.video (userInteractive) and com.solstream.audio (userInitiated) queues, which survive unchanged. Reassembly, decode submission and Opus decoding never run on the reader thread, so a 30-fragment video burst delays audio ingest by 30 AES-GCM opens (~40 us), not by a decode.

SEND SIDE, MAC: input is sealed and sendto'd on the thread that captured it. That deletes the single largest avoidable latency in the current design — ControlStream.swift:135-139 appends to an array under a lock and ControlStream.swift:221-285 calls enet_host_service(host, &event, 50), so an input event can sit 50 ms before it is even encrypted, 25-100x the network cost on this LAN.

PRIMITIVES: AES-256-GCM, HKDF-SHA256, HMAC-SHA256, ECDH P-256. All four already present on both machines. Package.swift stays dependencies: []. Nothing added, audited or licensed.

CHACHAPOLY REJECTED. BCrypt has no ChaCha20-Poly1305, so it means shipping several hundred lines of constant-time stream cipher and MAC on Windows to run a software cipher on a machine with AES-NI — both riskier and slower. The only thing it buys is a nonce wide enough to choose at random, which is precisely the property this counter construction is designed not to need. AES-256 over AES-128 because the key schedule amortises across a whole session and 14 vs 10 rounds is a rounding error against a 16.7 ms frame budget.
