THE TOKEN IS AN AUTHENTICATOR, NEVER A KEY. main.cpp:1239-1242 states plainly that the agent channel is plaintext TCP and the token authenticates the client and nothing else; AgentConnection.swift:387-396 sends it in the clear. Deriving media keys from it alone would hand every past and future session to anyone who ever watched one auth handshake.

REQUIRED FIRST: AGENT AUTH v2. Not a second pairing step, not a PIN, not user-visible — one extra field on a command that already exists. kProtocolVersion 1 -> 2 (main.cpp:70). hello gains "challenge":"<64 hex>" (32 bytes from the BCryptGenRandom already at main.cpp:1259). The Mac replies {"cmd":"auth","proof":"<64 hex>","cnonce":"<64 hex>"} where
  proof = HMAC-SHA256(tokenBytes, "SolStream agent auth v2" || challenge || cnonce)
and tokenBytes is the 16 raw bytes the 32 hex chars decode to. The host recomputes and compares with the constant-time compare already shaped at main.cpp:1311-1322. The legacy "token" field is still accepted so a v1 client works, but a v2 client REFUSES to start media against a v1 host. After this the token never appears on any wire. I would not ship the media path without this in the same commit.

DERIVATION, EXACTLY:

  tokenBytes = 16 raw bytes of the agent token
  canonicalParams = ASCII, built from the values in the HOST'S REPLY (not the
    request), so both sides agree on what was actually granted:
    "w=<w>;h=<h>;fps=<fps>;codec=<codec>;bitrateKbps=<n>;ch=<n>;rate=<n>;frameMs=<n>;window=<hex>"

  transcript = "SOLSTREAM-MEDIA-v1" || cpub(65) || cnonce(32)
             || hpub(65) || hnonce(32) || u64BE(hcount) || canonicalParams

  bindKey    = HMAC-SHA256(tokenBytes, "SolStream media binding v1")
  hostAuth   = HMAC-SHA256(bindKey, "host confirm"   || transcript)
  clientAuth = HMAC-SHA256(bindKey, "client confirm" || transcript)

  Z   = ECDH-P256 shared x-coordinate, 32 bytes BIG-ENDIAN (reverse BCrypt's)
  PRK = HKDF-Extract(salt = SHA-256(transcript), ikm = Z || tokenBytes)

  sid     = HKDF-Expand(PRK, "solstream v1 session id", 4) -> u32 BE
            sessTag = low byte of sid. sid is DERIVED on both sides and never
            transmitted, so there is no "which one is authoritative" question.
  chain_0 = HKDF-Expand(PRK, "solstream v1 chain 0", 32)

  for epoch e:
    okm = HKDF-Expand(chain_e, "solstream v1 epoch" || u32BE(e), 108)
    K_h2c = okm[  0.. 32]   host->Mac AES-256 key
    F_h2c = okm[ 32.. 38]   host->Mac 6-byte nonce fixed field
    K_c2h = okm[ 38.. 70]   Mac->host AES-256 key
    F_c2h = okm[ 70.. 76]   Mac->host 6-byte nonce fixed field
    chain_{e+1} = okm[ 76..108]
    then ZEROISE chain_e.

FOUR PROPERTIES, EACH LOAD-BEARING:
1. Both parties must know the token or hostAuth/clientAuth fail. An active MITM on the LAN without the token cannot substitute their own ephemeral: the transcript MAC covers both public keys, both nonces, hcount and the granted parameters.
2. The token is mixed into the HKDF IKM, not only into the transcript MAC. An adversary who obtains the token LATER cannot decrypt sessions recorded EARLIER. A token leak is total compromise going forward and nothing at all going backward — which is the property that matters against "has seen every previous session".
3. Per-direction keys. K_h2c != K_c2h always, so the nonce proof never has to reason about two senders sharing a key space. ControlStream.swift:315-320 gets this right today by convention (an ASCII "CC"/"HC" tag in the IV); this gets it right by key separation, so it does not depend on anyone remembering to set two bytes.
4. Forward secrecy WITHIN a session: chain_e is destroyed as soon as epoch e's keys and chain_{e+1} exist, so scraping host memory at epoch 7 yields nothing that decrypts epochs 0-6.

REKEYING is a pure ratchet — no negotiation, no round trip, no failure mode. The sender bumps the epoch nibble when its counter crosses 2^31 or after 10 minutes, whichever first. NIST SP 800-38D 8.3 caps a deterministic-nonce GCM key at 2^32 invocations; 2^31 leaves 2x headroom, and at 2500 pps the timer fires first (1.5M packets). The receiver holds epochs e-1 and e live, each with its own replay window, and retires e-1 one second after committing e. Design 1 signalled rekey with a CONTROL/REKEY message; a rekey that needs no message cannot fail to be delivered.

An attacker cannot drive the ratchet: the receiver derives candidate keys for e+1 WITHOUT deleting anything, attempts the open, and commits (zeroising chain_e, retiring e-1) only once a packet actually authenticates under e+1. Forward movement is capped at +1 per commit, so a forged nibble costs one speculative HKDF-Expand. The nibble is compared mod 16 accepting only e-1, e, e+1 — three live values of sixteen, so wrap is unambiguous forever and forces no re-handshake. A full re-handshake is nonetheless mandated every 24 hours.

REPLAY DEFENCE: per direction, per epoch, a 1024-slot sliding window as uint64_t bits[16] plus a highest-accepted watermark. Reject if counter <= watermark - 1024 or the slot is already set. DO NOT COPY THE EXISTING REFERENCE: udp_input.h:49 declares a single uint64_t m_bitmap commented "Bits 0..63" while clipboard_input_protocol.h:122 sets kReplayWindowSize = 1024, so 960 of the 1024 slots do not exist and `1ULL << diff` for diff in [64,1024) is undefined behaviour. Sixteen words is the fix.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT PROTECT AGAINST, STATED PLAINLY:
- Traffic analysis. Sizes and timing are in the clear and nothing is padded, because padding costs bandwidth and latency on the exact axis being optimised. An observer can tell when you are typing and roughly the bitrate. Encrypting the type byte raises the bar; it does not remove this.
- Anyone holding the token. It is a 128-bit bearer secret in a plaintext file at %LOCALAPPDATA%\SolStream\agent.token and, on the Mac, in UserDefaults (AgentConnection.swift:150-160) — an unprotected plist any process running as the user can read. That is the weakest link and this design raises the stakes on it; it should move to Keychain and DPAPI.
- Endpoint compromise, and a malicious host driving VideoToolbox with hostile bitstreams. Authenticity means "it is the host you paired with", not "the bytes are safe".
- DoS. A LAN attacker flooding 47631 costs one byte compare per forged packet (sessTag) and one AES-GCM verify per lucky one. A determined flooder degrades the stream. There is also a pre-existing DoS this does not touch: the agent serves one client and replies busy to a second (main.cpp:3951-4021), so whoever connects first locks the real Mac out.
- Full VM snapshot rollback of the host, which replays the RNG and hcount together. hcount defends the ordinary cases (a cloned image, a bad boot-time RNG seed) and explicitly not this one.
- Key commitment. AES-GCM is not key-committing. Not exploitable here (one key per direction, no attacker-chosen keys) but it is a property this construction lacks.
- The agent channel's own contents. Window titles, app names, the display layout and the entire clipboard still travel in plaintext TCP. The media is now encrypted and the channel describing your desktop is not. That is the largest remaining gap in the product, and the same handshake specified here could key an AEAD for it.
synthesis.nonceConstruction:
CONSTRUCTION. For direction d and epoch e, the nonce of the i-th Seal is

    N(d, e, i) = F(d, e) || BE48(i)

where F(d,e) is the secret 6-byte fixed field from the key schedule (never transmitted) and i is the 48-bit counter, starting at 0, carried verbatim in header bytes 2..7. Twelve bytes. This is the NIST SP 800-38D 8.2.1 deterministic construction: F is the fixed field, i is the invocation field.

Nothing is computed, nothing is reconstructed from a truncated field, and there is no window arithmetic that could put two packets on the same nonce. That is the entire reason the counter is carried at full width rather than truncated: five bytes per packet (about 100 kbps at 2500 pps, 0.5% of a 20 Mbps stream) buys the removal of a whole class of reconstruction bugs from the one place in the system where a bug is silent and catastrophic.

CLAIM: no (key, nonce) pair is ever used twice for encryption. Since a collision only matters under the same key, it suffices to show i never repeats within a fixed (d, e) of a fixed session, and that (d, e, session) never repeats a key.

(1) WITHIN ONE (d, e). i comes from a single 64-bit atomic per direction, laid out as epoch in bits 63..56, counter in bits 47..0, with bits 55..48 a permanently-zero guard band. A send does fetch_add(1) and uses the PRE-value; fetch_add on one atomic totally orders its own returns, so two sends cannot obtain the same value under any thread interleaving. When a pre-value crosses the 2^31 rekey threshold the sender CASes to (epoch+1, counter=0); threads that lose the CAS retry, threads that already hold a pre-value under the old epoch use it and are still unique because their i is distinct and their epoch is the old one. The guard band exists so a burst of concurrent fetch_adds during the CAS window cannot carry the counter into the epoch field: the distance from 2^31 to 2^48 is 2^47 increments, which no burst approaches. If i ever reached 2^48-1 the sender ABORTS THE SESSION rather than sealing. There is no wrap.

(2) ACROSS EPOCHS IN ONE SESSION. K(d,e) and K(d,e+1) are separate HKDF-Expand outputs from separate chain values, so a repeated i is harmless. F(d,e) also differs. Either fact alone suffices; both hold.

(3) ACROSS THE TWO DIRECTIONS. K_h2c and K_c2h are disjoint byte ranges of the same 108-byte HKDF-Expand output, so they differ; F_h2c and F_c2h likewise. Both senders may legitimately sit on counter 0 at the same instant and the (key, nonce) pair still differs in both components.

(4) ACROSS RECONNECTS. Every media open runs a fresh ECDH with fresh ephemerals on BOTH sides plus fresh 32-byte nonces on both sides. PRK depends on all four, so a repeated master secret requires both sides to repeat both their ephemeral and their nonce simultaneously — one side's RNG failing is not enough. The host additionally mixes hcount, a persisted u64 flushed to disk before use and monotonically increasing, so on the host side even total RNG failure yields a distinct transcript and therefore a distinct PRK. THERE IS NO SESSION RESUMPTION AND NO KEY CACHING: op:"resume" resumes application state and performs a completely fresh key exchange. It is a hard rule that no key material derived in one handshake is ever carried into another.

(5) ACROSS PROCESS RESTARTS. Master secrets live only in memory and are never written to disk. A restarted agent cannot re-derive an old one even if it wanted to, and a restart drops the agent TCP connection, which tears the media session down, which forces a new handshake. The host additionally refuses to install keys for a session whose derived sid matches one retired less than 5 seconds ago — that would be a demux annoyance rather than a nonce problem, but it is cheap to exclude.

(6) COUNTER EXHAUSTION. Bounded by (1). The 2^31 rekey fires 131,072 times before a 48-bit counter could be exhausted once, and the 10-minute timer fires long before that at any realistic rate. The 2^31 ceiling is itself half of SP 800-38D 8.3's 2^32 limit, so the standard's own bound is respected with a factor of two spare. The sender fails closed rather than repeating.

(7) RETRANSMISSION DOES NOT CONSUME A COUNTER — the clause design 2 did not need because it had no retransmission, and which grafting tier 1 makes mandatory. A NACK'd datagram is re-sent as the BYTE-IDENTICAL SEALED RECORD taken verbatim from the ring: same counter, same nonce, same ciphertext, same tag. It is never re-sealed. GCM's requirement is that one key never seal two DIFFERENT plaintexts under one nonce; re-sending an identical record leaks only that it was sent twice, which the network already reveals, and the receiver's replay window drops it. A RE-SEAL UNDER AN ALREADY-USED COUNTER WOULD LEAK THE XOR OF TWO PLAINTEXTS AND THE AUTHENTICATION KEY. This is the single most important invariant in the implementation: the retransmit path copies bytes and must never touch the cipher. It gets an assert in debug and a named test.

RECEIVER SIDE. The receiver never encrypts under a nonce derived from a received packet, so a forged counter cannot induce reuse. It selects a key by epoch nibble, rebuilds the nonce as F(d,e) || the six wire bytes, opens, and only then consults the replay window. A duplicate that authenticates is dropped by the window; one that does not is dropped by the tag. Neither path touches send-side state.

WHAT WOULD BREAK IT, SO IT CAN BE TESTED:
- Two threads sealing while reading the counter without the atomic. The whole argument reduces to "one key, one atomic"; that invariant belongs in a comment beside the counter declaration, not only in this document.
- A retransmit path that re-seals. Forbidden by (7).
- A future change that shares one key between two counters — a second socket, or a per-substream counter added for convenience.
- Persisting any part of PRK or a chain value. Nothing is persisted except hcount, which is not key material.

CONTRAST WITH WHAT EXISTS. ControlStream.swift:409-410 uses a bare uint32 that wraps with no rekey, is not bound to any session id, and therefore repeats every nonce from the beginning across any reconnect that reuses the key. Clauses (1), (4) and (6) are precisely the repairs.
synthesis.sequencingAndLoss:
TWO INDEPENDENT SEQUENCE SPACES, DELIBERATELY.

1. TRANSPORT COUNTER — the 48-bit per-direction counter in the outer header, monotonic across every packet the sender emits whatever its type. This is the loss detector and the NACK/retransmit index. Because it spans all substreams, loss is measurable even when video is idle on a static screen — which, with WGC's change-driven delivery, is the normal steady state rather than an edge case. A per-video sequence number cannot do this.

2. MEDIA STRUCTURE — frameId + fragOff for video, audioSeq for audio, baseSeq/evSeq for input. This is the damage locator.

GAP CLASSIFICATION. A gap at counter S is declared LOST when either
  highestCounter >= S + 8            (reordering beyond 8 does not happen on a
                                      LAN; at 2500 pps this fires in ~3 ms)
  or now - firstSeenAt > max(2 ms, RTT)
whichever is first. Both rules are required and the WGC finding is why the second is load-bearing rather than belt-and-braces: the threshold rule is useless whenever the packet rate is low, and a static window makes that the common case, not the rare one.

TIER 1 — BOUNDED RETRANSMIT (grafted from design 1; design 2 refused retransmission outright). This is the part a WAN protocol would not have and a LAN protocol should. RTT here is 0.5-2 ms against a 16.7 ms frame period, so a fragment NACK'd 2 ms after the gap opens arrives about 4 ms after it was lost, comfortably inside the same frame's assembly window. The frame is repaired with one packet and the user sees nothing.

  SENDER keeps a ring of the last 512 emitted SEALED datagrams, ring[counter & 511], with the counter stored for validation and sentAtUs[counter & 511] alongside. At 1450 bytes that is ~740 KB and about 200 ms of history at 2500 pps.
  RECEIVER NACKs a declared-lost counter AT MOST ONCE, and only if the frame it would repair has not passed its deadline. NACKs ride on an immediately-sent FEEDBACK, rate-limited to one out-of-band FEEDBACK per 4 ms.
  SENDER honours a NACK only if ring[counter & 511].counter == counter AND nowUs - sentAtUs < oneFramePeriodUs. Otherwise it ignores the NACK and lets tier 2 handle it.
  THAT DEADLINE TEST IS WHAT MAKES RETRANSMISSION INCAPABLE OF ADDING LATENCY: a frame past its display deadline was going to be dropped either way.
  The retransmitted datagram is byte-identical and is never re-sealed (nonce clause 7).

VIDEO REASSEMBLY. A frame is a buffer plus a received-interval list plus the flags seen. Each fragment is memcpy'd to base + fragOff; the receiver never assumes a fragment size, so the sender may change fragment size at any frame boundary when the MTU estimate moves, and there is no padding and therefore nothing to trim. Fragments almost always arrive in offset order, so the interval list holds one entry; cap it at 16 and declare the frame damaged on overflow, because a frame that arrived in 17 disjoint pieces is not worth saving.

A frame is closed and its verdict emitted at whichever comes first:
  - every byte in [0, totalLen) present, where totalLen = fragOff + payloadLen of
    the FRAME_END fragment -> DELIVER, synchronously, in the receive path;
  - a fragment of a higher frameId arrives -> close as damaged;
  - 25 ms since its first fragment -> close as damaged.
The timer is load-bearing BECAUSE OF WGC: a lost FRAME_END followed by a static window leaves the frame open indefinitely and the loss is never reported at all.

Frame numbering only moves forward. NO RESYNC HATCH IS NEEDED. VideoDepacketizer.swift:150-169's 96-packet escape exists solely to survive two encoders sharing a socket after a /resume; here a new session has new keys, so a previous encoder's packets cannot authenticate under the current key. That failure mode is deleted by the key schedule rather than worked around.

NO TRAILING-ZERO TRIM. VideoDepacketizer.swift:253-257 strips all trailing zero bytes to undo FEC block padding, which also eats legitimate trailing zero bytes of the last NAL. With no FEC and explicit AVCC lengths there is nothing to trim and the footgun cannot exist.

SLICE-EARLY TRANSMISSION. The encoder's slice-output callback calls the transport directly; the transport seals and sendto's inline. There is no queue between the encoder and the socket. A partial datagram is flushed at every slice boundary — about three extra short packets per frame at four slices (~4.7 KB/s) to save each slice waiting ~4 ms for the next to fill it. On a 1 ms LAN, 4 ms is not a rounding error.

HONEST LIMIT, WORTH STATING BEFORE ANYONE MEASURES: VideoDecoder.swift:124-141 submits one CMSampleBuffer per access unit, so slice-early transmission buys network pipelining only until VideoDecoder changes — roughly the serialisation time of a frame, ~340 us at 1 Gbps and ~3.4 ms at 100 Mbps. Pipelining the decode too is a separate change to VideoDecoder, not a transport change.

THE ONLY WAITS IN THE DESIGN, EXHAUSTIVELY:
  1. Filling a datagram to the path MTU from within one slice. Bounded by the encoder's own byte production, tens of microseconds, and it never crosses a slice boundary.
  2. The 2 ms reorder timeout before declaring a gap lost. A wait to COMPLAIN, not a wait to DECODE; it blocks nothing.
  3. The host's input reorder hold, <= 30 ms, when an event's predecessor is missing — and redundancy makes reaching it require R+1 consecutive losses.
  4. The tier-1 deadline window on an already-damaged frame, bounded by that frame's own display deadline.
REJECTED EXPLICITLY: waiting for frame completion before sending; pacing on a healthy path; batching audio frames; a service-loop tick before sending input; waiting for an ack before the next frame; holding a complete frame for A/V sync.

PACING VS BURSTING. Burst by default: a 40 KB frame is ~28 packets and takes 340 us at 1 Gbps, which cannot build a queue on a link carrying 20 Mbps, so pacing would only add delay. A pacer exists as a LOSS RESPONSE, not a default: when FEEDBACK shows lostPackets > 0 or measured goodput falls below the send rate, video fragments are spread over min(framePeriod, bytes / measuredRate). That is the Wi-Fi case and exactly where pacing earns its keep. The pacer gates VIDEO only — never audio, input, feedback, control or retransmits.

AUDIO. audioSeq gaps reset the Opus decoder so it does not interpolate across a hole, which StreamSession.swift:287-294 already does and is correct. With HAS_PREV armed a single-packet gap is filled from the redundant copy and no reset happens at all.

INPUT. baseSeq is per EVENT, so the host's dedup is exact and the redundancy window is expressible as "events baseSeq..baseSeq+count-1". The host applies strictly in evSeq order. Because every datagram carries the authoritative stateFlags bitmap and the current pointer position, the steady state is self-correcting before any explicit desync handling fires.

COPIES PER FRAME. Today: at least four (UdpStream.swift:159,192 -> VideoDepacketizer.swift:206 -> :215-219 -> VideoDecoder.swift:323-344). Here: recvmsg into a pooled buffer, decrypt in place, memcpy once into the frame buffer at fragOff, then one CMBlockBuffer construction. Two copies before the decoder, and AVCC means no start-code scan and no byte-at-a-time trim.

SOURCE-ADDRESS FILTERING IS DELETED. UdpStream.swift:181-207 rejects datagrams whose source does not match exactly — a real anti-injection measure and also a silent-failure hazard when the host's address changes. The AEAD is strictly better at both jobs: a forged packet fails authentication wherever it came from, and a legitimate packet from a new address authenticates. The old filter is not weakened by removal, it is subsumed.
synthesis.ltrFeedback:
THE POINT: replace "loss happened, send an IDR" with "loss happened, predict from a frame the client has TOLD me it holds". An IDR is 5-10x a P-frame, which is why ControlStream.swift:99-120 had to rate-limit IDR requests to 2/s — unthrottled requests turned loss into a bandwidth spike that caused more loss. An LTR-anchored P-frame is roughly P-sized. The recovery that used to be the expensive thing becomes the cheap thing, and the damper can be relaxed by an order of magnitude.

ltrHave IS THE SPINE (design 2). The client tells the host, 60 times a second, exactly which long-term reference frames it holds intact — an 8-bit bitmap in a packet it is already sending. The host never has to infer which old frame the client might still have; it reads a bitmap. Everything else falls out of that.

CLIENT STATE. lastGoodFrame (highest frameId received complete AND whose reference chain it actually holds), highestFrameSeen, damagedMask (64 bits, ~1.07 s at 60 fps, comfortably longer than the LTR window it interacts with), ltrHave (set when the frame that marked a slot arrived intact and was decodable; cleared when a slot is re-marked by a frame the client did not receive intact), ltrGen.

HOST POLICY. Eight slots, each MARKED / CONFIRMED / STALE. ONLY A CONFIRMED SLOT IS EVER USED AS A RECOVERY REFERENCE — the host is not guessing that the client has the frame, the client has said so. That is what makes recovery deterministic instead of hopeful, and it makes aggressive marking free: a marked-but-unconfirmed slot costs nothing and risks nothing.

Marking cadence: every 8 FRAMES, into the oldest slot that is NOT the client's currently-relied-on slot. Two grafts here. The never-overwrite-the-acked-slot rule is design 1's, and it is the invariant that guarantees a repair frame is always encodable. Counting in FRAMES rather than milliseconds is mine and it is a direct WGC consequence: a wall-clock cadence over a static window marks nothing for a minute and then marks a burst. Eight frames spans ~133 ms at 60 fps, so the table covers ~1.06 s, inside the damagedMask window.

FOUR TIERS.

TIER 1 — RETRANSMIT (0-4 ms, invisible). Specified under sequencing. On a LAN this absorbs the overwhelming majority of real loss with no encoder action at all, which is what demotes LTR from first line of defence to second and reserves it for losses that matter. Design 2 had no tier 1; grafting it is the single largest change I made to the spine.

TIER 2 — LTR-ANCHORED REPAIR FRAME (~one frame period). Triggered when tier 1 could not repair in time, or on REQUEST_LTR_RECOVERY.
  t+0      the client's reassembler closes frame F as damaged
  t+0      it sets REQUEST_LTR_RECOVERY and sends FEEDBACK immediately (the
           16 ms periodic report is not waited for; 4 ms floor)
  t+RTT/2  the host reads ltrHave and picks the NEWEST slot that is CONFIRMED,
           not named in damagedMask, and whose frameId <= lastGoodFrame
  t+RTT/2  the next frame is encoded predicting ONLY from that slot, with
           RECOVERY_POINT set, ref = that slot, and marked into a fresh slot
  t+~1frm  the client sees ref naming a slot in its own ltrHave and resumes
On a 1 ms LAN at 60 fps: ~16 ms detection (bounded by the frame period) + 1 ms + 16 ms, about 33 ms, one frame of bitrate, no spike. The IDR path it replaces was a 500 ms damper plus a 5-10x byte spike.
  DAMPER: one repair per 100 ms. A second report inside the window folds into the pending repair rather than queueing. The host ignores any request naming a frame it has already answered, so a burst of three identical reports costs one repair frame.
  Typical repair size 2-5x a P-frame, i.e. 5-20x smaller than an IDR. That ratio is the entire argument for LTR and it is why loss stops being self-amplifying.

TIER 3 — INTRA-REFRESH (passive backstop, no extra packets). Entered when three or more repairs are needed within one second, or client-reported loss exceeds 0.5% over a one-second window. A rolling band of intra macroblocks sweeps the picture over 30 frames (~500 ms). In this mode the host sends NO repair frames and ignores loss reports for recovery purposes; the picture self-heals within one sweep no matter what arrives. THIS IS THE TIER THAT KEEPS THE STREAM ALIVE WHEN THE FEEDBACK CHANNEL ITSELF IS BROKEN, which is the one case LTR cannot handle by construction. Sets hostFlags.DEGRADED so the quality pill can say so; RECOVERY_POINT marks the frame completing each sweep. Left after 3 s of zero loss (design 1's number, not design 2's 10 s) because it costs 10-20% efficiency and re-entering is cheap.

TIER 4 — IDR, LAST RESORT ONLY. Session start; RENEGOTIATE; no CONFIRMED slot survives (a loss burst spanning the whole window, or a client that just joined); DECODER_STALLED. Rate-limited to one per 500 ms — ControlStream.swift:35's damper kept verbatim, for the reason the code already gives. Always preceded by PARAMSETS and carrying PARAMSETS_INLINE.

THE MAC'S THREE EXISTING IDR PRODUCERS, RE-POINTED:
  depacketizer on an incomplete frame (StreamConnection.swift:962-964)
      -> tier 1 NACK, escalating to REQUEST_LTR_RECOVERY
  decoder with no parameter sets (VideoDecoder.swift:114-118)
      -> PARAMSETS_MISSING, which asks for ~60 bytes rather than a whole IDR;
         today an IDR every 0.5 s is a very expensive way to ship SPS/PPS
  decoder after a recoverable VT error (VideoDecoder.swift:219-227)
      -> REQUEST_IDR, because no reference frame helps a decoder with no session
  session watchdog after 1 s of no frames (StreamSession.swift:184-225)
      -> REWRITTEN. It must key on HOSTBEAT arrival, not frame arrival. With WGC,
         no frames is the normal steady state for a static window, so the existing
         watchdog would declare a healthy stream lost five times and give up.

DISCARDABLE (design 1). A frame nothing will reference can be lost with no consequence: the receiver does not report loss for it, does not NACK it, and does not break its chain. That removes an entire class of pointless repair frames on a path with light background loss.

BITRATE CONTROL, WHICH DOES NOT EXIST TODAY. StreamConnection.swift:801-802 pins min and max to the same configured value; there is no adaptation loop of any kind. Every 16 ms the host now has goodput (rxBytes/rxPackets), loss rate, jitterUs, frameAgeUs (true capture-to-display, from captureUs) and RTT from PING/PONG.
  additive increase +5% per second while loss < 0.1% and frameAgeUs is not trending up
  multiplicative decrease x0.85 on any 250 ms window with loss > 1%, OR when
    frameAgeUs rises more than 30 ms above its session floor
  floor 2 Mbps, ceiling from the session parameters, applied through the encoder's
    dynamic reconfigure, which needs no IDR
THE DELAY SIGNAL IS PRIMARY, NOT THE LOSS SIGNAL: a Wi-Fi or powerline bottleneck queues long before it drops, so a latency-first design must react to delay or it feels fine for the entire buffer-filling period and discovers the problem one full queue too late.
  GATED ON hostFlags.ENCODER_IDLE == 0. Mine, and neither design would survive without it: goodput measured across a static WGC window is not a network measurement, and an ungated controller would ratchet to the floor every time the user stopped typing.

END-TO-END LATENCY BECOMES MEASURABLE. captureUs on every frame and every audio packet, against RTT from PING/PONG, gives capture-to-display and capture-to-speaker on one clock. Today timestamps are fabricated locally at submit time (VideoDecoder.swift:350-354) and no host timestamp travels the wire, so there is currently no way to tell an encoder stall from a network stall from a decode stall. spike/wgc-capture/RESULTS.md says outright that the real capture latency "has to be re-measured end to end against an actual encoder, with the timestamp taken where the encoder emits its first slice" — captureUs is that timestamp.
synthesis.sessionSetupJson:
Everything happens on the agent's existing newline-JSON channel. The entire Sunshine setup path — HTTP pairing, HTTPS /launch or /resume, and the seven RTSP round trips at StreamConnection.swift:684-762 — is deleted and replaced by three lines.

STEP 0, AUTH v2 (must ship in the same commit). kProtocolVersion 1 -> 2 at main.cpp:70.

Host hello gains one field:
{"type":"hello","version":2,"host":"DEVBOX","needsAuth":true,"sunshineInstance":"0","challenge":"<64 hex = 32 random bytes>"}

Mac replies (still outside the FIFO, as AgentConnection.swift:387-396 does today):
{"cmd":"auth","proof":"<64 hex>","cnonce":"<64 hex = 32 random bytes>"}
  proof = HMAC-SHA256(tokenBytes, "SolStream agent auth v2" || challenge || cnonce)
Host: {"type":"auth","ok":true}  or  {"type":"auth","ok":false,"message":"bad token"}
The legacy {"cmd":"auth","token":"..."} is still accepted; a v2 client refuses to start media against a v1 host.

STEP 1, MEDIA OPEN. Mac -> host, after auth succeeds:

{"cmd":"media","op":"open","ver":1,
 "cpub":"<base64 of 65 bytes, 0x04||X||Y>",
 "cnonce":"<base64 of 32 bytes>",
 "cport":52341,
 "window":"0x00050A3C",
 "codec":["h264"],
 "w":2560,"h":1600,"fps":60,"bitrateKbps":20000,
 "audio":{"ch":2,"rate":48000,"frameMs":5},
 "mtuHint":1280}

`window` is the HWND to capture, as a hex string because HWND is 64-bit on Win64 and JSON numbers are doubles. This field is what the WGC spike makes possible and it is what removes the display-mode dance: the host captures the window, not a display.

The Mac binds its UDP socket BEFORE sending open and reports cport, so the host may send its first frame without waiting to hear from the Mac.

STEP 2, HOST REPLY:

{"type":"media","ok":true,"ver":1,
 "hpub":"<base64 of 65 bytes>",
 "hnonce":"<base64 of 32 bytes>",
 "hcount":"41",
 "port":47631,
 "w":2560,"h":1600,"fps":60,"psGen":1,
 "codec":"h264","bitrateKbps":20000,
 "audio":{"ch":2,"rate":48000,"frameMs":5},
 "mtuHint":1280,
 "hostAuth":"<base64 of 32 bytes>"}

hcount is a decimal string (u64 exceeds JSON's safe integer range), persisted beside agent.token, incremented and flushed BEFORE it is used. sid is NOT sent: both sides derive it from PRK, so there is no question of which is authoritative. The reply echoes every negotiated parameter because canonicalParams is built from the GRANTED values, not the requested ones — a request can be unachievable, exactly as the existing `canvas` command returns what it got rather than what was asked (main.cpp:2872-2884).

Failure: {"type":"media","ok":false,"reason":"<r>"} with reason in
  unsupported-version | bad-window | bad-key | busy | no-encoder | bad-params

STEP 3, CONFIRM. Mac verifies hostAuth against its own transcript. A mismatch means the peer does not know the token: drop the connection and do not retry, in the spirit of the existing impersonation check at AgentConnection.swift:839-850. On success:

{"cmd":"media","op":"confirm","clientAuth":"<base64 of 32 bytes>"}
-> {"type":"media","ok":true,"op":"confirmed"}

STEP 4. The Mac immediately sends SESSION/START on UDP. This is the path-establishment step and it is the important difference from what exists: the host learns where to send from a packet that AUTHENTICATES, not from the source address of a plaintext ping. Today the host latches the peer from whatever address an unauthenticated 20-byte ping arrived from (UdpStream.swift:5-12), which anyone on the LAN can forge. In SMT/1 there is no unauthenticated packet at all, in either direction, ever.

STEP 5. Host replies SESSION/START_ACK, sends PARAMSETS, starts the encoder. First video follows.

OTHER OPS:
{"cmd":"media","op":"resume","sid":"<base64 of 4 bytes>","cpub":"...","cnonce":"...","cport":52341}
  Reattaches encoder configuration, window and locks. OTHERWISE A COMPLETE FRESH
  HANDSHAKE: new ephemerals, new nonces, new hcount, new PRK, new sid, counters
  from zero. There is no cryptographic resumption in this protocol.
  -> {"type":"media","ok":false,"reason":"expired"} falls through to a full open.
{"cmd":"media","op":"stop"} -> {"type":"media","ok":true,"op":"stopped"}

COST: one TCP round trip (sub-millisecond on a LAN) plus one P-256 keygen and one ECDH per side (~50-100 us), against the current path's pairing, launch and seven RTSP exchanges.

THREADING CONSTRAINTS RESPECTED. The handshake is an ordinary command/reply pair through HandleCommand, so it takes one FIFO slot on the Mac (AgentConnection.swift:117-118) and one turn on the agent's single-client thread, and it is ~400 bytes of JSON against a 4 MiB kMaxLineBytes. It sits after the auth gate alongside `displays` and `windows`, rate-limited to one handshake per 250 ms so it cannot be used to make the agent thread do unbounded P-256 work.

CRITICALLY, ONCE IT COMPLETES THE MEDIA PATH NEEDS THE AGENT THREAD FOR NOTHING. Rekeying is a ratchet with no signalling. Renegotiation, keepalive, feedback and teardown are all in-band on UDP. That satisfies the constraint that a `launch` blocking the agent thread for up to 60 s (main.cpp:2932-2945) must not stall media, and it means the media path is unaffected by the cursor watcher's 40 ms pushes and the window watcher's 120 ms pushes. The media start handler does the ECDH, hands the derived keys to an independent subsystem with its own threads, and returns.

WHAT STAYS ON THE JSON CHANNEL AND WHY: cursor shape, window geometry, place, lock, topmost, focus, clipboard, apps, launch, displays. All human-cadence, none in the video path, and moving any of it onto the media socket would put variable-size payloads next to the frame stream for no latency gain. Cursor shape is the tempting exception and it stays: 40 ms is already below what a person notices, and it is pushed rather than polled precisely so it does not queue behind the place commands issued during a live resize (main.cpp:3140-3151).

TIMER CADENCES. Media timers are 16 ms (FEEDBACK), 100 ms (HOSTBEAT), 200 ms (Mac PING). Existing agent cadences are 40 ms (cursor), 120 ms (windows), 1.0 s (window status, clipboard), 10 s (heartbeat against a 30 s idle timeout). These are different threads and different sockets, so periodic coincidence is harmless — unlike the shared-reactor case that made the video and audio pings collide (UdpStream.swift:62-70).

WHERE THE SOCKET LIVES: in SolStream.exe, not in Sunshine. That is the structural point. The encoder, the packetizer and the socket move into the agent; spike/wgc-capture finally gets a consumer; and Sunshine, shipped unmodified because it is GPL-3.0, leaves the media path entirely.
synthesis.mtuAndReconnect:
MTU — PROBED, NOT ASSUMED, AND NEVER A REASON NOT TO START.

Base is 1280 bytes of IP datagram: the IPv6 minimum, and the number this tree already knows for Tailscale and WireGuard (StreamConnection.swift:35). The session always starts there so a small-MTU link produces a working stream immediately rather than a black window, which is what a fixed 1500 assumption gives you.

Video fragment payload = pathMTU - 28 (IPv4+UDP) - 8 (outer header) - 16 (tag) - 16 (video inner) = pathMTU - 68. So 1212 bytes at 1280 and 1432 at 1500. The 28 must be a named constant now, because it becomes 48 on IPv6.

Probing is packetization-layer and the HOST probes, because the host sends the large packets:
  - IP_DONTFRAGMENT (Windows) / IP_DONTFRAG (Darwin) is set, so an oversized probe
    is dropped rather than fragmented. Otherwise a probe "succeeds" via IP
    fragmentation and you adopt an MTU that turns every video fragment into two IP
    fragments with double the effective loss rate.
  - the probe is a PING with MTU_PROBE set, zero-padded inside the ciphertext to
    the candidate size;
  - PONG reports rxSizeBytes, so the host confirms the size actually arrived
    intact rather than inferring it from an ack;
  - ladder 1280 -> 1400 -> 1452 -> 1472, three probes per rung, adopt on the first
    success, stop at the first rung that fails all three;
  - re-probe every 60 s and immediately after any path migration.
ICMP is not relied on: it is filtered, rate-limited and forgeable.

BLACK-HOLE DETECTION. If loss on the current fragment size exceeds 20% for 500 ms while the smaller PING/FEEDBACK traffic flows cleanly, drop straight to 1280 and restart the ladder. That asymmetry — small packets fine, large packets gone — is the signature of an MTU that shrank, and it must be detected explicitly because otherwise it looks exactly like congestion and the bitrate controller chases it forever.

Fragment size changes at the next frame boundary. The receiver never assumes a fragment size, so a mid-frame change would be harmless; the boundary rule keeps the sender's packetizer simple. --packet-size (main.swift:59-67) survives as a manual floor override.

NAT REBINDING AND PATH MIGRATION.

Receiving: THE AEAD IS THE FILTER. A datagram is accepted from any source address if it authenticates under the current inbound key and passes the replay window.

Sending: migration is separate and gated, because "send to wherever the last good packet came from" is exploitable — an on-path attacker can copy a genuine authenticated datagram and race it in from a spoofed source to redirect the stream. Design 1 re-latched on any authenticated advancing packet; design 2's challenge is strictly better and costs one RTT on a real rebind, so:
  - the peer address is reconsidered only on a packet that authenticates AND
    carries a counter strictly greater than any previously accepted, so a
    replayed packet is inert for migration;
  - even then, send a PING with PATH_CHALLENGE and 8 random bytes to the NEW
    address and keep sending media to the OLD one until a PONG echoing those
    bytes arrives from the new address. Only the real peer can echo, because the
    challenge is inside the ciphertext;
  - one migration per second, so an attacker cannot make the host thrash;
  - cost on a genuine rebind: one round trip, 0.5-2 ms.
No UDP amplification vector exists: the handshake is on TCP and the host never sends media to an address that has not completed a challenge.

RECONNECT, FOUR CASES.

(a) MEDIA SILENT, AGENT UP. Declared dead after 3 s with no authenticated packet (the Mac pings every 200 ms, so 15 consecutive losses). Fresh media open: new ephemerals, new PRK, new sid, counters from zero. One RTT plus a P-256 keygen, under 5 ms. The windows are NOT torn down — today recovery means closing the windows and building a new session (main.swift:616-620) because StreamSession cannot be restarted in place; here session identity lives in the transport and survives.

(b) AGENT TCP DROPS. The media session dies with it, because its keys came from that session. TWO HOST CHANGES ARE REQUIRED and both are worth stating because the current behaviour is destructive: closing the agent socket runs UnlockAll(), which pulls every streamed window off the virtual display back onto the real desktop in the middle of a session the user is watching — and main.cpp's own comment on the oversized-line path says exactly this, that dropping the connection is far more destructive than it sounds. So (1) hold window locks and encoder state for a 10 s grace period keyed to sid, and (2) a Mac that reconnects inside that window gets its windows back where they were.

(c) RESUME. op:"resume" with the old sid reattaches encoder configuration, window and locks, and is otherwise a complete fresh handshake. NO KEY, CHAIN VALUE, COUNTER OR NONCE FIXED FIELD EVER SURVIVES A SESSION BOUNDARY. This is what makes nonce clause 4 hold and it is precisely the flaw the current control stream has (ControlStream.swift:409-410).

(d) BOTH GONE. Reconnect the agent with its existing backoff machinery, re-auth, op:"open" from scratch.

HOST EXPIRY: no authenticated client datagram for 3 s and the host stops the encoder, frees the session and zeroises the keys. At 5 PINGs/s that is 15 consecutive misses. The old session's keys are also zeroised the moment a new handshake completes. Late packets from a retired session cannot decrypt under the new key and are dropped at the AEAD with no special-case code — which is what deletes the two-encoders-on-one-socket resync hack at VideoDepacketizer.swift:150-169.

TEARDOWN: SESSION/STOP repeated three times over ~2 ms (cheap insurance on a lossy path) plus {"cmd":"media","op":"stop"} on the JSON channel, which is reliable and therefore authoritative. Today teardown blocks up to 0.4 s to get TERMINATION on the wire and then ALSO calls HTTPS /cancel, because TERMINATION alone left the host reporting BUSY and locking out every later client (StreamConnection.swift:328-338). Here the reliable path is a line on a socket that is already open, so the blocking wait disappears; and the 3 s expiry means even kill -9 on the Mac cannot wedge the host.

RENEGOTIATION ON RESIZE — a genuinely new capability. main.swift:562-566 states the canvas is fixed for the life of a session, so today a Mac window resize is a HOST-WINDOW resize inside a fixed canvas driven by `place`. SESSION/RENEGOTIATE goes IN-BAND ON UDP, deliberately not on the agent channel, because a live resize drag already saturates that channel with `place` and a renegotiation queued behind them would arrive after the drag ended. Repeated every 20 ms until acked. The host reconfigures the encoder, recreates the WGC frame pool, bumps psGen, sends PARAMSETS then an IDR, and replies RENEG_ACK with what it actually achieved. The client rebuilds its VideoToolbox session on the parameter-set change, a path it already has and exercises (VideoDecoder.swift:99-105). Self-clocked: at most one outstanding, superseded rather than queued, mirroring the discipline AppWindow.swift:403-427 already applies to `place`; below a 5% area change the Mac scales locally instead of asking, so a drag produces a handful of reconfigures rather than sixty IDRs.

Frame-pool recreation on resize is open question 3 in spike/wgc-capture/RESULTS.md and RENEGOTIATE depends on it directly.

The 4096-per-axis clamp stays (main.swift:420-422): an NVENC H.264 limit, reachable on ordinary hardware, and above it the handshake succeeds and no frame ever arrives. The host validates it in RENEGOTIATE and refuses with a result code rather than accepting and going silent. Per-window capture makes it far less likely to be hit, since the canvas is now a window rather than a 16-inch MacBook Pro's 4112x2658.

PAUSE. FEEDBACK's WINDOW_HIDDEN flag stops the encoder outright when the Mac's window is occluded or minimised. The agent already detects and pushes occlusion. Costs nothing and is the largest single power and thermal win available on the host. Note it is NOT needed for host-side occlusion any more: the spike proves WGC keeps delivering at an unchanged latency distribution while the target window is fully covered, which is what makes the virtual display driver unnecessary.
synthesis.borrowedFrom:
FROM DESIGN 2 (SMT/1) — THE SPINE:
- The 8-byte cleartext outer header and the 48-bit counter carried at full width.
- The nonce: secret 6-byte fixed field || counter verbatim. Nothing reconstructed.
- The whole key schedule: transcript, bindKey, PSK-into-IKM, the 108-byte per-epoch HKDF-Expand with per-direction keys and fixed fields plus a chain that is zeroised, and the ratchet with speculative-then-commit epoch acceptance.
- hcount, persisted and flushed before use, so a host with a broken RNG still derives distinct keys.
- ltrHave and the MARKED/CONFIRMED/STALE slot model. The best single idea in either document, and the reason recovery is deterministic rather than hopeful.
- The two-sequence-space split: transport counter as loss detector, media structure as damage locator.
- PING/PONG with txUs and turnaroundUs, so RTT is a network measurement rather than a scheduling measurement.
- Strict-priority datagram-granularity scheduling, and the one-reader-thread demux.
- Path migration behind a PATH_CHALLENGE, rate-limited.
- The MTU ladder with DF set, PONG carrying rxSizeBytes, and black-hole detection.
- The 25 ms frame-closure timer.
- INPUT with stateFlags, no MOUSE_MOVE event type, and event redundancy instead of ARQ.
- Audio HAS_PREV redundancy.
- The honest threat-model enumeration and the agent-channel grace period on reconnect.

FROM DESIGN 1 (SSMT) — THE GRAFTS:
- TIER 1 BOUNDED RETRANSMIT with the sender-side deadline test. Design 2 refused retransmission on principle; on a link where RTT is a tenth of a frame period that principle costs a repair that would have been invisible. The deadline test is what makes it safe.
- fragOff, a byte offset, instead of a fragment index — because slice-boundary flushing makes fragments variable-length.
- captureUs at microsecond resolution instead of captureMs.
- The DISCARDABLE flag.
- PARAMSETS_INLINE ahead of every IDR, on top of the out-of-band repeat-until-acked.
- The never-overwrite-the-client's-acked-LTR-slot marking rule.
- The 3 s exit from intra-refresh (design 2 said 10 s).
- HOSTBEAT's existence as a concept (design 1 had an idle heartbeat; design 2 had none) and inputAck/inputMiss.
- The observation that the retransmit path must copy a sealed record and never re-seal, which becomes nonce proof clause 7.
- The framing of "the only waits in the entire design, exhaustively", which is a good discipline and is reproduced.

MINE, FROM READING THE TREE:
- HOSTBEAT's ENCODER_IDLE and lastFrameId, and the rewrite of StreamSession's watchdog to key on HOSTBEAT rather than frames. WGC delivery is change-driven (241 frames for 240 paints; a still window costs nothing), so "no frames" is a normal steady state and the existing watchdog would declare a healthy stream lost.
- LTR marking cadence counted in frames, not milliseconds, for the same reason.
- Bitrate control gated on ENCODER_IDLE == 0, because goodput measured across a static window is not a network measurement.
- psGen in the video header, so a frame cannot be decoded under parameter sets that replaced it.
- A fixed 16-byte video inner header instead of design 1's conditional one: the saving is 0.5% and the cost is a differently-parsed header on the path carrying 97% of the bytes.
- evSeq widened to u32.
- The `window` HWND field in the media open JSON, which is what per-window WGC capture needs and what makes the display-mode ladder unnecessary.
- sid derived on both sides and never transmitted.
- canonicalParams built from the host's granted values rather than the client's requested ones.
- sessTag justified as a 256x DoS prefilter rather than only as a demux aid.
- The build order, which is arranged so the encoder unknown is measured at step 6 rather than assumed at step 1.

VERIFIED IN-TREE WHILE WRITING THIS, NOT TAKEN ON TRUST FROM THE SURVEY:

- Package.swift:14 is dependencies: [], with CEnet and CCommonCrypto as local targets.

synthesis.conflictsResolved:
1. HEADER WIDTH — design 2's 8-byte header with a full 48-bit counter over design 1's 4-byte header with the epoch packed into the top two bits: a nonce you can read straight off the wire needs no reconstruction, and 4 bytes per datagram is 0.28% at a 1500 MTU.

2. RETRANSMISSION — design 1's bounded tier 1 over design 2's blanket refusal: on a link where RTT is a tenth of a frame period a repair lands inside the same frame's assembly window, and the sender-side deadline test makes it provably incapable of adding latency.

3. FRAGMENT ADDRESSING — design 1's byte offset over design 2's fragment index: slice-boundary flushing makes fragments variable-length, so an index does not tell the receiver where to put the bytes.

4. VIDEO HEADER SHAPE — a fixed 16 bytes over design 1's conditional 7-or-15: saving 0.5% is not worth parsing the header differently on the path that carries 97% of the bytes.

5. REFERENCE RECTANGLE IN INPUT — design 2's per-packet refW/refH over design 1's session-level constant: a renegotiation in flight would otherwise scale a queued input event by the wrong rectangle, and 4 bytes at input rates is under 1 kB/s.

6. TIMESTAMPS — design 1's u32 microseconds over design 2's u16 milliseconds: 1 ms quantisation is coarser than the RTT being measured.

7. TAG POSITION — design 2's tag-at-the-end over design 1's tag-before-ciphertext: the sender encrypts in place in one buffer with the tag landing in the trailing bytes, and the ciphertext starts 8-byte aligned instead of at offset 20.

8. REKEY SIGNALLING — design 2's silent ratchet nibble over design 1's CONTROL/REKEY message: a rekey that needs no message cannot fail to be delivered.

9. PATH MIGRATION — design 2's PATH_CHALLENGE over design 1's re-latch-on-any-authenticated-advancing-packet: an on-path attacker can copy a genuine datagram and race it in from a spoofed source, and the challenge costs one RTT on a real rebind.

10. AUDIO LOSS — design 2's HAS_PREV redundancy over design 1's do-nothing: 60 bytes at 200 pps when armed turns a single-packet loss from an audible 5 ms hole into nothing, and it is redundancy, not FEC.

11. INTRA-REFRESH EXIT — design 1's 3 s of clean loss over design 2's 10 s: the mode costs 10-20% efficiency and re-entering it is cheap.

12. evSeq WIDTH — u32 over design 1's u16: a u16 wraps in about a minute of scrolling and forces wrap arithmetic into the host's dedup path.

13. MTU CONFIRMATION — design 2's PONG rxSizeBytes over design 1's mtuMask bits in FEEDBACK: confirming the size that actually arrived beats inferring it from an acknowledgement.

14. sid — derived on both sides and never transmitted, against design 2 sending it in the reply: a value that is both derived and transmitted creates a question about which one is authoritative.

15. PER-PACKET AEAD ON THE MAC — CommonCrypto in-place over CryptoKit AES.GCM, with the caveat that this is a preference to be settled by measurement at build step 3 rather than an assertion: AES.GCM.open allocates a fresh Data per call and at 2500 pkt/s that is 2500 allocations per second on the userInteractive queue.

16. NO CONFLICT, BOTH RIGHT, RECORDED BECAUSE IT IS NON-NEGOTIABLE: both designs demand challenge-response auth v2 before media keys derive from the agent session, and both are correct. It ships in the same commit as the transport, not after it.
buildOrder: 1. CROSS-LANGUAGE CRYPTO VECTORS, NO SOCKETS. HKDF-Extract/Expand, the transcript, hostAuth/clientAuth, sid, the per-epoch 108-byte expansion, the nonce construction, and one sealed packet of each type. A Windows console test and a Swift test that both print the same hex to stdout. MEASURE: byte-for-byte agreement, and specifically that the BCryptDeriveKey(BCRYPT_KDF_RAW_SECRET) little-endian reversal is right. This is the bug whose only symptom is a black window, and it is far cheaper to find in a vector test than on a wire. Nothing else may start until these agree.

2. AGENT AUTH v2, ALONE AND SHIPPABLE. kProtocolVersion -> 2, hello.challenge, auth.proof, legacy token still accepted. MEASURE: a v2 Mac authenticates against a v2 host; a v1 Mac still authenticates; tcpdump on 47630 no longer contains the token. Independently valuable, independently shippable, and the media path must not ship before it.

3. TRANSPORT CORE WITH PING/PONG ONLY. One socket on 47631, 8-byte header, AEAD, the counter atomic, the 1024-slot replay window as uint64_t[16], the epoch ratchet, PATH_CHALLENGE, and the MTU ladder. No media of any kind. MEASURE, and these are the first real numbers this project will ever have: RTT min/p50/p95 over 60 s against the dev box; sustained packets/s on one reader thread; per-datagram AEAD cost on both ends; that a forced rekey at a deliberately low threshold survives; that the replay window rejects all 1024 slots and not 64. This also settles CommonCrypto vs AES.GCM by measurement instead of argument.

4. THE media AGENT COMMAND AND SESSION. Handshake through HandleCommand, SESSION START/START_ACK/STOP over UDP, host 3 s expiry, and all four reconnect cases. Still no media. MEASURE: wall clock from media open sent to START_ACK received, against a target of one RTT plus ~100 us of P-256; that a launch blocking the agent thread for 60 s does not disturb an established session; reconnect time for each of the four cases; that the agent-drop grace period returns windows where they were.

5. VIDEO HOST-TO-MAC FROM A FILE SOURCE. Packetizer, AVCC framing, byte-offset reassembly, frame closure, driven by a pre-encoded H.264 file rather than a live encoder so the transport is measured without the encoder as a variable. Feeds the existing VideoDecoder unchanged. MEASURE, and this is where the repository's total absence of measured sizes finally ends: real slice-size distribution, fragments per frame, IDR-to-P size ratio, reassembly cost, copies per frame, and behaviour under dnctl/pfctl induced loss at 0.1%, 1% and 5% with reordering and duplication.

6. WGC ENCODER INTO THE TRANSPORT, SLICE-EARLY. Wire spike/wgc-capture to a hardware encoder and to the packetizer. MEASURE: capture-to-first-slice-on-the-wire in microseconds, which RESULTS.md explicitly says still has to be measured and explicitly says the 17 ms median is not; and whether the encoder exposes LTR slot marking and per-slot reference selection at all. That second one is the largest unknown in the design and it gates tier 2 — if it is absent, tier 2 collapses into tier 3 and the design still works, but recovery goes from one P-frame to half a second of intra-refresh. Do task #14 (WGC against a swap-chain app) before this step, not after.

7. AUDIO AND INPUT. Opus over AUDIO with HAS_PREV, INPUT with stateFlags and the redundancy window, host-side evSeq-ordered SendInput applier, HOSTBEAT with inputAck/inputMiss. MEASURE: real Opus packet sizes (recorded nowhere in the tree), real mouse-event rate (InputCapture counts it and no value has ever been written down), and key-to-pixel latency against the current path's 50 ms enet_host_service quantisation, which is the number this whole exercise exists to beat.

8. FEEDBACK, THEN TIER 1, THEN LTR, THEN RATE CONTROL, IN THAT ORDER. Each is measurable only once the one before it works. MEASURE: what fraction of induced loss tier 1 absorbs with no encoder action at all (the hypothesis is most of it on a LAN); repair-frame size against IDR size; visible glitch duration per tier; and that the rate controller does not ratchet to the floor when ENCODER_IDLE is set, which is the specific WGC failure this design guards against.

9. DELETE, ONLY AFTER 1-8 MEASURE WELL. Sources/CEnet (~10k lines of vendored C), ControlStream.swift, UdpStream.swift, VideoDepacketizer.swift, InputProtocol.swift, the RTSP/HTTP/SDP setup inside StreamConnection.swift, and ClientIdentity.swift / CertificateFactory.swift / ServerTrust.swift, since no certificates are needed once keys come from the agent session. This is task #13 and it should stay blocked until step 8 produces numbers. Deleting it earlier removes the only working reference to compare against.
openQuestions: DOES THE ENCODER EXPOSE LTR AT ALL? This gates tier 2 and it is the largest unknown in the design. Nothing in SolStream configures an encoder — sunshine_host.cpp:550-591 writes no encoder keys whatsoever — so there is no evidence in the tree about slot count, per-frame reference control, or whether marking needs a full reconfigure. Answered by measurement at build step 6, not by reading source. If it is two slots with no per-frame control, the LTR window shrinks to ~260 ms and the 33 ms recovery figure evaporates; the design degrades correctly and degrades badly in the terms it was sold on.

IS THE COMMONCRYPTO GCM ONE-SHOT AVAILABLE IN THE macOS 14 SDK? The design's contract is one AEAD open per datagram decrypting in place into a pooled buffer. CommonCrypto through the already-vendored Sources/CCommonCrypto is the preferred implementation because AES.GCM.open allocates a fresh Data per call; whether the one-shot symbols are exposed must be checked against the SDK. Fallback is AES.GCM with the allocation cost measured at build step 3.

THE THREE OPEN QUESTIONS IN spike/wgc-capture/RESULTS.md THAT THIS TRANSPORT DEPENDS ON. (a) Swap-chain and DirectComposition applications — the old display-capture path rendered Windows Terminal as a solid black rectangle, and terminals and browsers are the applications worth streaming. Task #14 exists for this and must land before build step 6. (b) Minimised windows, which decides whether CAPTURE_LOST is a real state or an impossible one. (c) Frame-pool recreation on resize, which SESSION/RENEGOTIATE depends on directly. Everything in RESULTS.md was measured on Windows 11 only.

IPv4 ONLY, INHERITED DELIBERATELY. UdpStream is AF_INET only (UdpStream.swift:73, 96-103) and the agent listener is AF_INET only with an IPv4-only --bind parser (main.cpp:3753, 3769-3775). SMT/1 as specified inherits that. The 28-byte IPv4+UDP constant in the MTU arithmetic becomes 48 on IPv6 and should be a named constant from the first commit even though dual-stack is deferred.

TWO PER-WINDOW CAPTURE IMPLEMENTATIONS NOW EXIST AND ONLY ONE SHOULD SURVIVE. windows/CaptureHelper already does per-HWND WinRT Graphics Capture into a D3D11 shared-texture ring with a named-pipe protocol and is consumed by nothing; spike/wgc-capture is newer and is what proved the borderless and occlusion properties. Deciding which is the basis for the host encoder is a prerequisite to build step 6, not a detail of it.

SHOULD THE TOKEN MOVE TO KEYCHAIN AND DPAPI? The key schedule limits a leak's blast radius to sessions after it, but the strongest link in the chain is anchored to a 128-bit bearer secret sitting in a plaintext file at %LOCALAPPDATA%\\SolStream\\agent.token and in an unprotected UserDefaults plist on the Mac (AgentConnection.swift:150-160). This is worth more than any refinement to the protocol.

THE AGENT CHANNEL ITSELF STAYS PLAINTEXT. Window titles, application names, the display layout and the entire clipboard still travel in the clear on TCP 47630 after this lands. The media will be encrypted and the channel describing the user's desktop will not. The same handshake specified here could key an AEAD for it; that is out of scope for this document and should not stay unaddressed.

EVERY QUANTITATIVE CLAIM HERE IS ARITHMETIC, NOT MEASUREMENT. The 512-entry retransmit ring, the reorder threshold of 8, the 64-frame damagedMask, the 8-frame LTR cadence, the 16 ms feedback period and R = 3 are all reasoned from configured defaults. The header fields are sized with enough slack to survive being wrong; the cadences will need retuning after build step 5.

ONLY TWO DESIGNS WERE SUPPLIED, NOT THREE. The brief says three independent designs; the array contains two entries (SSMT and SMT/1). If a third exists I have not seen it and nothing from it is reflected here.

findings.title: The v1 auth fallback turns an unauthenticated `hello` into a token-disclosure oracle
findings.sequence: 1. Attacker ARP-spoofs the host's IP on the LAN (or simply wins the race on the Mac's next automatic reconnect — AgentConnection already reconnects with backoff). 2. Attacker accepts the TCP connection on 47630 and sends `{"type":"hello","version":1,"host":"DEVBOX","needsAuth":true,"sunshineInstance":"0"}` — i.e. no `challenge` field. 3. The design mandates "The legacy {\"cmd\":\"auth\",\"token\":\"...\"} is still accepted so a v1 client works", so the v2 Mac, finding no `challenge`, takes the legacy path and calls `authenticate(with: token)` at AgentConnection.swift:387-396, writing the 32 hex chars to the socket in the clear. Nothing gates this: AgentConnection.swift:821-823 reads `version` and only logs it, and the only downgrade check in the file (AgentConnection.swift:839-850) fires on `needsAuth:false`, not on a missing challenge. 4. Attacker now holds tokenBytes. 5. With tokenBytes the attacker computes bindKey, hostAuth, clientAuth AND the `Z || tokenBytes` HKDF-Extract input, so it can MITM or originate every future media session, and can issue `launch` on the host.
findings.consequence: Total, permanent compromise of a 128-bit bearer secret that the design elevates from "authenticates the client" to "root of all media key material". Property 2 of the key schedule (a token leak compromises nothing backward) survives, but everything forward is gone, including the encrypted media path this whole design exists to build. The design's central claim — "After this the token never appears on any wire" — is false for any session where the peer says it is v1.
findings.fix: Delete the client-side legacy path entirely. The Mac must never emit `{"cmd":"auth","token":...}` under any circumstance: if `hello` lacks a `challenge`, report "this PC is running an older SolStream agent" and drop the connection without reconnecting, exactly as AgentConnection.swift:839-850 already does for `needsAuth:false`. Host-side acceptance of legacy tokens may remain for other clients; the disclosure is entirely on the client's side of the wire.

findings.title: Auth v2 is unilateral and unbound, so it relays: an attacker gets an authenticated agent session without the token
findings.sequence: 1. Attacker ARP-spoofs the host and accepts the Mac's TCP connection. 2. Attacker simultaneously opens its own TCP connection to the real host and receives the real host's `challenge` C. 3. Attacker sends C to the Mac as its own `hello.challenge`. 4. Mac replies `{"cmd":"auth","proof":HMAC(token, "SolStream agent auth v2" || C || cnonce),"cnonce":N}`. 5. Attacker forwards `proof` and `cnonce` verbatim to the real host, which recomputes and accepts. 6. The attacker now holds a fully authenticated agent session it obtained without ever knowing the token, and simultaneously controls the Mac's view of the channel. It can issue `launch`, read `clipboard`, and drive `place`/`lock`/`focus`/`topmost` on the host, and can rewrite or drop anything the Mac sends. The media handshake still resists it — the attacker cannot produce clientAuth or the PRK, because tokenBytes is in the HKDF IKM — but the agent channel is fully owned.
findings.consequence: Arbitrary process launch and clipboard exfiltration on the Windows host from a LAN position with no secret at all. Auth v2 is presented as the prerequisite that makes the media keys trustworthy; as specified it proves only that *someone* who knows the token is reachable, never that the peer knows it, and it binds to no channel or key, which is precisely what makes relay work.
findings.fix: Bind the agent channel to a key a relay cannot derive. Every primitive is already specified: run the P-256 ECDH and the transcript MAC immediately after auth v2 rather than at `media open`, and AEAD-wrap (or at minimum MAC) every subsequent newline-JSON line under a key expanded from the same PRK. Because tokenBytes is in the IKM, a relay derives no key and its authenticated session is unusable at the first command. This also closes the acknowledged "the agent channel itself stays plaintext" gap for free.

findings.title: The epoch used to select the AEAD key is not specified to come from the fetch_add pre-value, and a 20-minute session reaches nonce reuse if it does not
findings.sequence: The spec says only "A send does fetch_add(1) and uses the PRE-value", never that the epoch must also be taken from that pre-value. The natural implementation is `uint64_t pre = ctr.fetch_add(1); uint48 c = pre & MASK; auto key = keys[currentEpoch];`. Then: 1. Thread A does fetch_add and holds pre = (e, 1500000); it is preempted before reading `currentEpoch`. 2. The 10-minute rekey timer fires on thread B, which CASes the atomic to (e+1, 0) and sets `currentEpoch = e+1`. 3. Thread A resumes, reads `currentEpoch` = e+1, and seals a video fragment with nonce F(d,e+1) || BE48(1500000) under K(d,e+1). 4. Ten minutes later, epoch e+1's own counter climbs through 1500000 in the ordinary way and a different plaintext is sealed with the identical nonce under the identical key. Both counters are ~1.5M because both epochs are ended by the same 10-minute timer at the same packet rate, so the raced value falling inside the next epoch's range is likely, not exotic.
findings.consequence: AES-GCM nonce reuse: the XOR of two plaintexts, and recovery of the GHASH authentication key H, which lets the attacker forge arbitrary authenticated datagrams in that direction — including INPUT packets to the host. Reachable in roughly 20 minutes of an ordinary session, with no attacker action required to trigger it; the attacker only has to be listening. This is the exact failure the nonce section is written to prevent, left open by an omission in the one sentence that defines it.
findings.fix: State it as a hard rule and assert it: the epoch used for key and fixed-field selection MUST be `pre >> 56` from the same fetch_add return value, never a separately-read variable. The layout already colocates them in one word specifically so this is possible; the spec just has to require it, next to the comment it already mandates beside the counter declaration.

findings.title: canonicalParams cannot be constructed as specified — `window` is absent from the host's reply, so either the handshake never completes or the capture target is unbound
findings.sequence: 1. canonicalParams is defined as `w=..;h=..;fps=..;codec=..;bitrateKbps=..;ch=..;rate=..;frameMs=..;window=<hex>` and is explicitly required to be built "from the values in the HOST'S REPLY (not the request), so both sides agree on what was actually granted". 2. The STEP 2 host reply enumerated in the design contains hpub, hnonce, hcount, port, w, h, fps, psGen, codec, bitrateKbps, audio{ch,rate,frameMs}, mtuHint, hostAuth — and no `window`. 3. The Mac therefore has no granted value to put in that field. Either it uses its requested window while the host uses the one it actually resolved (a stale HWND, or a fallback after `bad-window` handling), the transcripts differ, hostAuth fails to verify, and the Mac drops the connection and does not retry per STEP 3 — a hard failure on the common case of a window that moved; or the implementer resolves the contradiction the obvious way and drops `window` from canonicalParams, at which point which window is being captured is bound by nothing.
findings.consequence: Path one: media never starts whenever the host does not capture the exact HWND requested, and the failure is indistinguishable from a bad token. Path two: the field the whole per-window design turns on is outside the transcript, so nothing in the handshake commits the host to capturing the window the user asked for, and the `window` value travels the plaintext TCP channel with no integrity protection.
findings.fix: Add `"window":"<hex>"` to the STEP 2 host reply alongside the other echoed grants, build canonicalParams from the reply on both sides as the spec already demands, and have the Mac abort if the granted window differs from the one it requested. One field, and the stated rule then holds without exception.

findings.title: The transport counter is documented as monotonic but resets to zero at every rekey, while every consumer of it is specified without an epoch
findings.sequence: 1. A session runs for ten minutes; the host's send counter reaches ~1,500,000. 2. The rekey timer fires and the sender "CASes to (epoch+1, counter=0)". 3. The Mac's gap detector, whose rule is `highestCounter >= S + 8` against a single per-direction highestCounter, now sees counter 0 after 1,499,999. 4. FEEDBACK.rxCounter is a bare `u48` with no epoch field, so the Mac reports 0 having just reported 1,499,999, and the host's view of what the Mac has received jumps backward by 1.5M. 5. FEEDBACK's NACK entries are `[u48 startCounter][u8 run]` with no epoch, so a NACK issued for a lost pre-rekey counter and one for a post-rekey counter are indistinguishable on the wire; only the `ring[c & 511].counter == c` check keeps the sender from retransmitting the wrong record, and that check is doing load-bearing work the spec never credits it with.
findings.consequence: A spurious loss burst reported at every rekey (every ten minutes), feeding the bitrate controller's multiplicative decrease and the tier-2/tier-3 escalation logic; and a NACK space that is ambiguous by construction on a design whose stated invariant is that the counter "is monotonic across every packet the sender emits whatever its type".
findings.fix: Do not reset the counter on rekey — let it run monotonically across epochs for the life of the session, and track packets-since-rekey in a separate variable for the 2^31 threshold. Nonce uniqueness is unaffected because both K(d,e) and F(d,e) change at the epoch boundary, and the counter then actually is what the design says it is. A 48-bit counter at 2500 pps lasts 3570 years, so nothing is lost.

findings.title: `sid` is specified as derived-and-never-transmitted, then transmitted in the clear by `op:"resume"`
findings.sequence: 1. The design states sid "is NOT sent: both sides derive it from PRK, so there is no question of which is authoritative", and justifies the 8-bit sessTag as "8 bits of a truncated secret, so it is not a stable cross-session identifier an observer can correlate on". 2. `{"cmd":"media","op":"resume","sid":"<base64 of 4 bytes>",...}` puts all 32 bits of sid on the plaintext TCP channel. 3. A passive LAN observer reads it, and now holds a stable identifier that links the pre-drop session's datagrams (via sessTag) to the post-resume session's, which is exactly the correlation sessTag's width was chosen to prevent. 4. The host also acts on that 32-bit value — restoring window locks and encoder state from the 10 s grace period — before the new handshake's clientAuth has been verified.
findings.consequence: The stated privacy rationale for sessTag is defeated across every reconnect, and a value derived from PRK is published for no benefit. Not directly exploitable for key recovery (HKDF-Expand outputs under distinct info strings are independent), but it contradicts a stated invariant, and invariants that are stated and then violated are the ones implementers rely on.
findings.fix: Replace the transmitted sid with a dedicated resume ticket that is not derived from PRK — e.g. `resumeId = HKDF-Expand(PRK, "solstream v1 resume ticket", 16)` from the *previous* session, used once and discarded. Keep sid derived and unsent as specified, and require the host to defer restoring locks and encoder state until clientAuth verifies.

findings.title: sessTag's claimed 256x DoS prefilter provides no reduction against the LAN attacker the threat model assumes
findings.sequence: 1. The design justifies sessTag partly as "rejecting 255/256 of a forged flood with a byte compare instead of an AES-GCM verify — a real 256x DoS cost reduction". 2. sessTag is a fixed byte at offset 1 of every datagram, in the clear, for the life of the session. 3. The attacker is stipulated to be on the same LAN. It sniffs one datagram, reads byte 1, and writes that byte into every packet of its flood. 4. Every forged packet now costs a full AES-256-GCM verify over up to 1448 bytes plus, for packets carrying nibble e+1, a speculative HKDF-Expand.
findings.consequence: A security property claimed in the design is worth exactly nothing against the attacker the design says it is defending against; it only filters a blind off-path flooder, which is not the stated threat. The risk is that the claim is believed and no real rate limiting is built.
findings.fix: Drop the DoS justification and keep sessTag only for its honest job, O(1) demux. If forged-flood cost matters, cap AEAD verifies per source per interval and drop past the cap — a byte compare on a value the attacker can read will never do it.

findings.title: The host is permitted to install keys and start the encoder before clientAuth is verified
findings.sequence: 1. The design says in STEP 2 that "the host may send its first frame without waiting to hear from the Mac", and in STEP 5 that the host starts the encoder after SESSION/START — but clientAuth is not verified until STEP 3, and nothing states that key installation and encoder start are gated on it. 2. An attacker holding a relayed agent session (see the relay finding) sends its own `media open` with its own cpub/cnonce and a cport it controls. 3. The host performs the ECDH, installs keys, allocates the encoder, and begins capture and transmission. 4. The attacker never sends `op:"confirm"`. The session occupies the encoder and the single-client agent slot until the 3 s expiry, and can be re-driven every 250 ms (the stated handshake rate limit). The attacker cannot decrypt anything — tokenBytes in the HKDF IKM defeats it — but it can hold the host's capture pipeline.
findings.consequence: Encoder and WGC frame-pool churn driven by an unconfirmed peer, and denial of the single client slot to the real Mac. The design asserts "No UDP amplification vector exists" and "the host never sends media to an address that has not completed a challenge"; the first still holds because the destination IP is pinned to the TCP peer, but the second is contradicted by STEP 2's first-frame-without-waiting.
findings.fix: State the ordering as a hard rule: the host installs keys, allocates the encoder and emits its first datagram only after clientAuth verifies. Delete the "may send its first frame without waiting" clause — it saves under a millisecond on a LAN and it is the sentence that opens this.

findings.title: sessTag demux across a reconnect drops the new session outright on a 1-in-256 collision
findings.sequence: 1. The Mac's media path drops and reconnects; the design explicitly accounts for "the brief window where an old and a new session coexist during reconnect" and gives sessTag as the demux key. 2. The new session's derived sid has the same low byte as the retiring one — probability 1/256, so roughly once every 256 reconnects. 3. The receiver demuxes an incoming datagram by sessTag to a single session context, picks the wrong one, the AEAD open fails, and the datagram is dropped. 4. Every datagram of the new session is dropped this way until the old context is torn down, i.e. until the 3 s expiry fires.
findings.consequence: A three-second black window on roughly one reconnect in 256, presenting as an intermittent unexplained stall that will be extremely hard to reproduce deliberately. The design already says "The tag is always the authority; sessTag is never trusted for anything", but a single-candidate demux does trust it.
findings.fix: On a sessTag match, attempt the open against every live session context, not just the first — there are at most two, and the second attempt only ever runs on the 1/256 collision, so the cost is nil.

attacks.verdictOnDesign:
The nonce construction survives. I attacked clauses (1) through (7) directly — reconnect, process restart, both directions, epoch wrap, counter exhaustion, retransmission, and reordering across a rekey — and found no way to force a repeat of a (key, nonce) pair as specified. F(d,e) || BE48(i) with per-epoch, per-direction key AND fixed field separation is genuinely robust: a repeated counter across epochs is harmless twice over, and a repeated counter across directions is harmless twice over. Mixing tokenBytes into the HKDF-Extract IKM rather than only into the transcript MAC is the single strongest decision in the document and it is what defeats every token-less MITM I tried against the media path, including one that relays the agent channel end to end. The replay window at uint64_t[16] is correct, and authenticating before consulting it is the right order. The choice to reject ChaChaPoly is well argued and I would not overturn it.

The breaks are all at the trust boundary the crypto hangs from, and two of them are serious. The critical one is that the design mandates backward compatibility with a v1 host while leaving the v1/v2 decision to an unauthenticated `hello` — which makes the Mac hand its token to anyone who says "I am old". That single sentence undoes the document's own claim that the token never appears on any wire, and it is worth noting that the existing code already gets the structurally identical `needsAuth:false` case right at AgentConnection.swift:839-850, so the pattern for the fix is already in the tree. The second is that auth v2 authenticates in one direction only and binds to nothing, so it relays, handing a LAN attacker `launch` and `clipboard` on the host with no secret at all. The media keys resist that attacker, but the design treats agent auth v2 as the foundation the media keys stand on, and a foundation that relays is not one.

Two further issues are underspecification rather than error: the epoch used for key selection is never tied to the fetch_add pre-value, which is the one omission that can still produce GCM nonce reuse in an otherwise sound construction; and canonicalParams names a field the host's reply does not carry, so the handshake as written cannot be implemented consistently by two independent teams — which matters more than usual here, because the failure mode the document itself identifies for a key-derivation mismatch is a black window with no diagnostic.

The document is unusually honest about what it does not protect (traffic analysis, the plaintext agent channel, the token at rest, key commitment) and I found no dishonesty in those sections. My recommendation on build order: the fix for finding 1 belongs in build step 2, not later, and build step 1's cross-language vector test should include a negative vector for the epoch-from-pre-value rule in finding 3 — it is the only finding here whose symptom is silent.

findings.title: Every recovery tier needs the encoder to emit a frame, and the design's own WGC finding says it won't
findings.sequence: 1. User stops interacting; WGC goes change-driven-idle (RESULTS.md: 241 frames for 240 paints, "a still window costs nothing"). 2. The last frame emitted before the window went still, frame N, loses one fragment. 3. Receiver's 25 ms frame-closure timer fires, closes N damaged, sets REQUEST_LTR_RECOVERY, sends FEEDBACK. 4. Host reads ltrHave, picks a CONFIRMED slot, and prepares to encode "the next frame ... predicting ONLY from that slot". 5. There is no next frame. WGC delivers nothing because nothing painted. 6. Escalation to tier 3 does not help: intra-refresh is "a rolling band of intra macroblocks sweeps the picture over 30 frames" — 30 frames that will never be produced. Tier 4 is an IDR, which is also a frame.
findings.consequence: A corrupt or stale picture persists for as long as the user does not cause a paint — unbounded, and in the common case of reading a document or watching a static window, seconds to minutes.
