The design's headline recovery numbers (33 ms tier 2, 500 ms tier 3) are all conditioned on a frame rate that the design elsewhere proves is zero in the steady state. This is the single largest gap: the author correctly identified that WGC delivery is change-driven and then applied that insight only to HOSTBEAT, the watchdog, LTR cadence and rate control — not to the recovery path, which is the one place it is fatal.
findings.fix: The host must be able to force a frame from the last captured surface. Keep the most recent WGC frame's texture alive; on REQUEST_LTR_RECOVERY, REQUEST_IDR, or on entering intra-refresh while ENCODER_IDLE is set, re-submit that retained texture to the encoder immediately, and keep re-submitting at the frame rate until the sweep completes or the client's lastGoodFrame advances past the repair. One retained texture and one 'force encode' entry point; no protocol change.

findings.title: A lost final key-up is a permanently stuck, auto-repeating key: no redundancy, no gap, no inputAck
findings.sequence: 1. User types 'a' and releases it, then stops typing (reading, thinking — the normal case). 2. The Mac sends the KEY_UP in INPUT datagram k. Datagram k is the last one; no k+1 is ever generated, so the R=3 redundancy window that would have repeated the event never gets a carrier. 3. Datagram k is lost. 4. The host's gap detector never fires: baseSeq gaps are detected by receiving a *later* datagram, and there is no later datagram. inputMiss is never set. 5. stateFlags self-healing ("a lost key-up self-heals at the next input packet") never fires, for the same reason. 6. The Mac's only cross-check is HOSTBEAT's inputAck — but the user was typing into a window that repaints, so video is flowing, and HOSTBEAT is specified as "sent every 100 ms *whenever no VIDEO datagram went out* in the last 100 ms". No HOSTBEAT is sent. inputAck never arrives. 7. Windows holds 'a' down and auto-repeats.
findings.consequence: Exactly the failure InputCapture.swift:328 already names in a comment — "Windows auto-repeats a key it never sees released, so a single missed key-up types forever". At 1% packet loss this happens roughly once per 100 typing bursts. It is unrecoverable inside the protocol; the only escape is the user moving focus away (releaseHeldInput) or generating more input, and generating more input while a key auto-repeats is exactly when it does the most damage. The design's claim that redundancy makes ARQ unnecessary holds only in the interior of an input burst, never at its tail — and every burst has a tail.
findings.fix: Two lines. (a) After the last INPUT datagram, the Mac re-sends a state-only INPUT (count=0 plus stateFlags plus lastEvSeq) at +10, +30 and +80 ms, then stops; ~16 bytes ×3 per burst. (b) Make HOSTBEAT unconditional at 100 ms rather than only-when-video-is-idle (24 bytes × 10/s = 240 B/s) so inputAck is always flowing and the Mac can detect a stalled evSeq and resend. Fix (b) is required anyway — see the HOSTBEAT finding.

findings.title: Repair frames are never repaired: the tier-2 suppression rule deadlocks on a lost repair
findings.sequence: 1. Frame 100 is damaged. Client sets REQUEST_LTR_RECOVERY with lastGoodFrame=99 and sends FEEDBACK. 2. Host encodes repair frame R predicting from a CONFIRMED LTR slot, with RECOVERY_POINT set. A repair is stated to be 2-5x a P-frame, so at a 7 KB P-frame that is 15-35 KB = 10-25 datagrams. 3. R loses a fragment (at 1% packet loss, P(damaged) ≈ 1-0.99^20 ≈ 18%). 4. Client's lastGoodFrame is still 99. Its next FEEDBACK, 16 ms later, sets REQUEST_LTR_RECOVERY naming lastGoodFrame=99 again. 5. "The host ignores any request naming a frame it has already answered." It ignores it. 6. Repeat forever, at 60 requests/s, all ignored.
findings.consequence: Deadlock until the tier-3 entry condition trips, and tier 3's own condition is "three or more repairs *needed* within one second" — if the host counts repairs it *sent* rather than requests it received, it never trips at all and the picture stays broken permanently. If it counts requests, the escape is a 500 ms intra-refresh sweep. Either way, the design's central claim — that LTR turns recovery from 500 ms into 33 ms — is false for the ~18% of repairs that are themselves damaged, which at 1% loss is the majority of the loss the tier exists to handle (repair frames are 2-5x the size of the frames they repair, so they are 2-5x more likely to be hit).
findings.fix: Suppress on *confirmation*, not on *request*. The host records repairFrameId when it emits R and clears the suppression when either the client's lastGoodFrame >= repairFrameId (it landed) or 100 ms elapses without that (it did not, send another). One extra field on the host's LTR state; no protocol change.

findings.title: Tail-fragment loss bypasses tier 1 entirely — the frame is closed damaged in the same instant the gap becomes visible
findings.sequence: 1. Frame N is a 7 KB P-frame: 5 datagrams at a 1432-byte payload, counters S-4..S. 2. The last datagram, counter S, carrying FRAME_END, is lost. 3. Gap detection rule A (highestCounter >= S+8) cannot fire: there are no more packets in frame N, and in the host→Mac direction the only other traffic is HOSTBEAT (10/s, suppressed while video flows) and PONG (5/s). 4. Gap detection rule B (now - firstSeenAt > max(2 ms, RTT)) cannot fire either: firstSeenAt is the moment the gap is *observed*, and a gap at the tail is not observed until a counter > S arrives. There is nothing to start the 2 ms timer. 5. 16.7 ms later, frame N+1's first fragment arrives. The gap at S becomes visible — and in the same instant the rule "a fragment of a higher frameId arrives -> close as damaged" closes frame N. 6. The receiver "NACKs a declared-lost counter ... only if the frame it would repair has not passed its deadline". The frame is already closed. No NACK is sent. Straight to tier 2.
findings.consequence: 1 in 5 to 1 in 6 of all video losses (whatever fraction lands on a frame's final datagram) skips the 4 ms tier-1 repair the design is built around and pays the full tier-2 cost: ~16.7 ms to notice, +RTT, +16.7 ms for the repair frame — 35-50 ms and one repair-frame-sized bandwidth spike, versus the 4 ms and one datagram that tier 1 promised. The build-order hypothesis at step 8 ("what fraction of induced loss tier 1 absorbs — the hypothesis is most of it") will measure materially worse than expected, and the measurement will not explain why.
findings.fix: Two changes, both receiver-side. (a) On receiving a fragment of frameId > N while N is incomplete, NACK N's missing counters *before* deciding N's verdict. (b) Do not close N damaged on the higher-frameId rule alone; hold it for max(RTT + 2 ms, 4 ms) first, then close. This delays only an already-damaged frame's verdict, never a healthy frame's delivery, and it is bounded by the tier-1 repair window that already exists.

findings.title: HOSTBEAT is suppressed exactly when video is flowing, which breaks the watchdog it was invented to fix
findings.sequence: 1. Stream is perfectly healthy: 60 fps of video flowing continuously. 2. HOSTBEAT is specified as "sent every 100 ms whenever no VIDEO datagram went out in the last 100 ms". No HOSTBEAT is ever sent. 3. The design also specifies: "session watchdog after 1 s of no frames -> REWRITTEN. It must key on HOSTBEAT arrival, not frame arrival." 4. Implemented as written, StreamSession.checkLiveness sees no HOSTBEAT for the entire session, waits stallThreshold, fires requestKeyframe up to maxKeyframeRequests times, then reports .lost — on a stream that is working.
findings.consequence: The rewritten watchdog is the exact inverse of the bug it was written to fix. Separately and independently: inputAck and inputMiss ride only on HOSTBEAT, so during any period of continuous video — i.e. whenever the user is actually interacting — the Mac gets zero input acknowledgement and has no way to detect a lost input event. That is the enabling condition for the stuck-key finding above.
findings.fix: Send HOSTBEAT unconditionally every 100 ms. It is 24 bytes plus 24 bytes of framing = 480 B/s, against a 20 Mbps stream. Then the watchdog rule is simply "no VIDEO and no HOSTBEAT for 400 ms", which is correct in both directions, and inputAck is always live. The conditional emission saves nothing measurable and costs two correctness properties.

findings.title: No encoder latency constraint is stated anywhere, and the largest single latency term in the system is left to the encoder's defaults
findings.sequence: 1. Build step 6 wires spike/wgc-capture to "a hardware encoder" with no configuration constraints given anywhere in the design. 2. The encoder is configured with a default (non-low-latency) preset: B-frames enabled, rate-control lookahead enabled. 3. With 2 B-frames, the encoder cannot emit frame N's slices until it has captured N+1 and N+2 — the encoder holds 2 frame periods = 33 ms before the first slice of N reaches the transport. With an 8-frame lookahead that becomes 133 ms. 4. On the Mac, VideoDecoder.swift passes _EnableTemporalProcessing to VTDecompressionSessionDecodeFrame, so VideoToolbox additionally holds output for reorder: another frame period. 5. The transport's entire measured latency budget — 12 us of scheduler priority, 340 us of serialisation, 4 ms tier-1 repairs — is invisible underneath it.
findings.consequence: 33-166 ms of purely encoder-side latency, unbudgeted and unmentioned, dwarfing everything the transport does. Worse, B-frames break three of the design's own structural rules: output order != decode order, so frameId is no longer monotonic in display order; "close frame N as damaged when a fragment of frameId > N arrives" misfires on every reordered frame; and frameAgeUs (capture -> presented) becomes meaningless as a congestion signal, which then feeds the bitrate controller.
findings.fix: State it in the header spec as a hard constraint the receiver may assume: zero B-frames, zero lookahead, zero-latency rate control, one slice-output callback per slice, and a VBV/HRD buffer of one frame period. Add it to build step 6 as a measured precondition (capture-to-first-slice-on-the-wire, which RESULTS.md already says must be measured). On the Mac, drop _EnableTemporalProcessing once the constraint holds.

findings.title: The pacer, as specified, blocks inside the hardware encoder's slice-output callback for up to a full frame period
findings.sequence: 1. The design states "the encoder's slice-output callback calls the transport directly; the transport seals and sendto's inline. There is no queue between the encoder and the socket." 2. It also states the pacer engages on loss: "video fragments are spread over min(framePeriod, bytes / measuredRate)". 3. FEEDBACK reports lostPackets > 0. Pacer engages. 4. Next slice callback fires with a 40 KB frame against a 20 Mbps measured rate: the transport spreads it over 16 ms — inside the callback, because there is no queue to spread it in. 5. The encoder's output thread is blocked 16 ms. The next WGC frame arrives at +16.7 ms with the callback still occupied. 6. The pipeline is now permanently one frame period behind, and it entered that state precisely when the link was already degraded.
findings.consequence: Adds a full frame period (16.7 ms at 60 fps) of encoder-side latency, and does so only under loss — the condition where the design most needs to not compound the problem. The design is also internally contradictory about whether the send path has a queue at all: 'strict priority at DATAGRAM granularity' over a 'send queue' cannot coexist with 'there is no queue between the encoder and the socket', and the 12 us worst-case audio delay is computed from the first while the slice-early argument is built on the second.
findings.fix: Resolve the contradiction in favour of one dedicated sender thread with per-class priority rings. The encoder callback seals the datagram (cheap, ~1-2 us) and enqueues it, then returns immediately. The pacer, the retransmit ring and the priority scheduler all live on the sender thread. This costs one queue hop of a few microseconds on the video path and makes both the priority claim and the never-block-the-encoder claim true at the same time.

findings.title: One lost packet in the first IDR costs 500 ms of black window, because the tier-4 damper is applied from session start
findings.sequence: 1. Session starts. Host sends PARAMSETS, then the first IDR with PARAMSETS_INLINE. 2. One fragment of the IDR is lost — a 200 KB IDR at a 1280-byte starting MTU (the design deliberately starts at 1280, not 1500) is ~170 datagrams, so at 1% loss this happens 82% of the time and at 0.1% loss 16% of the time. 3. The Mac has parameter sets (PARAMSETS arrived) but no decodable picture. 4. No LTR slot is CONFIRMED — the session just started — so tier 2 is unavailable by its own rule. Tier 3 needs a reference to refresh from. It falls to tier 4, IDR. 5. Tier 4 is 'rate-limited to one per 500 ms — ControlStream.swift:35's damper kept verbatim'. An IDR was sent at t=0. 6. The repair IDR is not sent until t=500 ms.
findings.consequence: Half a second of black window at connect, on a single lost packet, on a LAN — the first thing a user sees. The damper was written for a protocol where an IDR request was the *only* recovery mechanism and unthrottled requests caused a bandwidth spiral; carried over verbatim into a design where tier 4 is the last resort, it throttles the one case where there is no alternative. The same applies mid-session on DECODER_STALLED after a VideoToolbox session loss.
findings.fix: Exempt the damper when the client has nothing to fall back on: if lastGoodFrame == 0, or no LTR slot is CONFIRMED, or DECODER_STALLED is set, send the IDR immediately and *then* start the 500 ms window. Cap the exemption at two consecutive IDRs so a client stuck in a decode failure loop still cannot spiral.

findings.title: The bitrate controller's delay signal ratchets to the floor on a clean LAN from clock drift alone
findings.sequence: 1. frameAgeUs is computed as capture -> presented, from captureUs (host monotonic microseconds) against the Mac's presentation time. Nothing in the design estimates or corrects the offset between the two machines' monotonic clocks. 2. The rule is "multiplicative decrease x0.85 ... when frameAgeUs rises more than 30 ms above its session floor". A relative measure, so the constant offset cancels — but the *drift* does not. 3. Two independent crystals at ±25 ppm each: up to 50 ppm relative. 50 ppm × 600 s = 30 ms. 4. At t = 10 minutes on a perfectly idle LAN with zero loss, frameAgeUs has drifted 30 ms above the session floor recorded at t = 0. 5. The controller applies x0.85. The session floor is a session floor; it never re-baselines. 6. At t = 20 minutes, x0.85 again. Bitrate reaches the 2 Mbps floor in about 90 minutes of a flawless connection, and the additive +5%/s increase cannot win because the delay term is primary and permanently violated.
findings.consequence: Video quality collapses over the course of a long session with no network cause and no diagnostic that would point at the clock. This is a slow version of exactly the failure the ENCODER_IDLE gate was added to prevent, and the gate does not catch it because the encoder is not idle.
findings.fix: Replace 'session floor' with the minimum frameAgeUs over a rolling 10 s window. Drift within 10 s is 0.5 ms at 50 ppm, i.e. below the noise. This is one ring buffer of 600 samples at the 16 ms feedback cadence and it makes the signal drift-immune without any clock synchronisation protocol.

findings.title: Slice-early transmission delivers approximately zero end-to-end latency benefit as specified, and its stated justification is arithmetically wrong
findings.sequence: 1. Send side does work as advertised: the encoder's slice callback seals and sends, so slice 0's bytes are on the wire before the frame finishes. That part of the design is sound. 2. Receive side gates on frame completion: "every byte in [0, totalLen) present, where totalLen = fragOff + payloadLen of the FRAME_END fragment -> DELIVER". Slice 0's bytes sit in the reassembly buffer until the frame's last byte arrives. 3. VideoDecoder.swift builds one AVCC buffer from all pictureNALs and submits one CMSampleBuffer per access unit, so even if the transport delivered slices, the decoder would not consume them. 4. Now compare the two send schemes at the last byte, which is what completion depends on: with slice-boundary flushing, the frame's final byte leaves the host the instant the encoder produces it. Without flushing — packing across slice boundaries — the frame's final byte also leaves the instant the encoder produces it, because the last datagram is short either way. Identical. 5. The design's claim, "to save each slice waiting ~4 ms for the next to fill it", describes a saving on slice 0's *arrival*, which no consumer uses.
findings.consequence: Three extra datagrams per frame (180 pkt/s at 60 fps) and ~10% more packets per frame, hence ~10% more chance of paying a repair, in exchange for a benefit the receiver cannot cash. The one real residual benefit is that a loss in slice 0 becomes visible to the gap detector earlier, so the tier-1 round trip overlaps the rest of the frame's encode instead of extending past it — worth having, but it is a loss-recovery argument, not the latency argument the design makes.
findings.fix: Either keep slice flushing and re-justify it honestly as earlier loss detection (and drop the 4 ms claim), or make the benefit real by delivering complete slices to the decoder as they arrive — which requires VideoDecoder to submit per slice, an explicitly separate change the design already flags. Do not pay for it twice: pick one and say which.

findings.title: Audio latency is designed to the millisecond in front of a 50-120 ms ring buffer the design never looks at
findings.sequence: 1. The design gives AUDIO top send priority (justified as saving ~1.2 ms at 10 Mbps), arms HAS_PREV redundancy at 37% audio overhead to turn a single loss from a 5 ms hole into nothing, and explicitly rejects two-frame bundling because it would cost 5 ms. 2. Frames are handed to AudioRenderer.playAudio, which writes into AudioRingBuffer, constructed with targetMilliseconds: 50 and ceilingMilliseconds: 120. 3. The buffer is trimmed only when filled exceeds the 120 ms ceiling, and then only back to the 50 ms target. 4. Steady-state audio latency is therefore somewhere in 50-120 ms depending on where jitter left the fill level, set by nothing in particular.
findings.consequence: Every millisecond-scale audio decision in the transport is being made 40-100x below the noise floor of the path it feeds. captureUs is added to the AUDIO header and, unlike video, nothing in the design ever consumes it — there is no clock recovery, no drift correction against the host's audio clock, and no A/V sync mechanism at all, so lip-sync is whatever the two ring fill levels happen to be.
findings.fix: Use the captureUs the header already carries: drive the ring's trim target from measured arrival jitter (target = p99 inter-arrival gap + one frame, floor 10 ms) instead of a hardcoded 50 ms, and add it to build step 7's measurement list alongside the Opus packet sizes. Until that is measured, the audio priority and HAS_PREV arguments should not be presented as latency wins.

attacks.verdictOnDesign:
The transport core is sound and the send path genuinely does put slices on the wire before a frame completes — the encoder slice callback seals and sends inline, so that requirement is met. But the benefit stops at the wire: the receiver gates delivery on FRAME_END plus every byte present, and VideoDecoder submits one CMSampleBuffer per access unit, so end-to-end the pipelining is worth roughly zero and the design's "saves each slice waiting ~4 ms" claim does not survive arithmetic (the frame's last byte leaves the host at the same instant either way). The design is honest that the decoder is the limit and then quotes the number anyway.

The serious problems are not in the microsecond accounting, which is mostly right — no reliability layer means no head-of-line blocking, the strict-priority claim holds at datagram granularity, and the input send path genuinely deletes the existing 50 ms enet_host_service quantisation. The serious problems are in the recovery path, and they cluster around one root cause: the author correctly discovered that WGC delivery is change-driven and then applied that insight to HOSTBEAT, the watchdog, LTR cadence and rate control while leaving it out of the place it is fatal. Tiers 2, 3 and 4 all recover by encoding a frame, and a static window produces no frames — so a loss on the last frame before the screen goes still is unrecoverable for an unbounded time. The same class of blind spot produces the stuck-key defect (redundancy has no carrier at the tail of an input burst, and HOSTBEAT's inputAck is suppressed exactly when video is flowing) and the tail-fragment defect (both gap-detection rules need a later packet, and the later packet closes the frame damaged in the same instant, so ~17% of losses skip tier 1 entirely).

Three further items are worth as much as any of the above. The tier-2 suppression rule deadlocks when the repair frame is itself lost, which at 1% loss is roughly one repair in five, and repair frames are 2-5x P-frame size so they are the *most* likely thing to be hit. The 500 ms IDR damper, carried over verbatim from a protocol where it made sense, throttles the one recovery that has no alternative at session start. And the largest single latency term in the entire system — encoder B-frames and lookahead, worth 33-166 ms — is not constrained anywhere in the document; a design that argues over 12 us of scheduler priority should not leave that to a preset default, particularly since B-frames also break frameId monotonicity, the close-on-higher-frameId rule, and frameAgeUs as a congestion signal all at once.

Finally, the bitrate controller's delay signal has no clock-drift correction and its session floor never re-baselines, which ratchets quality to the 2 Mbps floor over about 90 minutes of a flawless connection. Every one of these has a small fix; none requires rethinking the wire format, the key schedule or the nonce construction, which are the parts of this design I have no complaint about.

findings.title: The last input event before the user goes idle is never repeated, never acked, and never noticed — permanent stuck key
findings.sequence: In a game or a text editor on the host: press and hold W (KEY_DOWN, evSeq 10). Walk for 20 s. Release W (KEY_UP, evSeq 11) — this datagram is lost. Now touch nothing. (1) Redundancy cannot save it: the design repeats "the last R key/button events" on subsequent datagrams that carry events, and there are none — the user has stopped typing. A pure mouse move is defined as count=0, so even wiggling the mouse carries no repeats. (2) stateFlags cannot save it: the bitmap is b0 shift, b1 ctrl, b2 alt, b3 meta, b4..b8 mouse buttons. Ordinary keys are not in it. (3) The host's gap detector cannot fire: it detects a hole in baseSeq, which requires receiving evSeq 12 to notice 11 is missing. There is no evSeq 12. (4) The 30 ms inputMiss and 100 ms desync timers are both keyed to that same gap and never arm. W is held down forever. The same sequence with a mouse button (press, drag, release-lost, then stop moving) sticks the button, because stateFlags only self-heals on the *next* datagram and there is no next datagram. InputCapture.swift:326-328 already documents the consequence in this exact codebase: "Windows auto-repeats a key it never sees released, so a single missed key-up types forever."
findings.consequence: The single failure mode the requirements name by name ("a keydown after its keyup is a stuck key") is reachable with one lost packet and zero subsequent activity. On Windows it is worse than a stuck key: auto-repeat turns it into an unbounded flood of characters or a character walking into a wall until the user manually presses and releases the same key. At 40% Wi-Fi loss the whole redundancy argument reduces to R+1 consecutive losses being unlikely — but here R is effectively 0, so a single loss does it, roughly every other keystroke-ending-a-burst.
findings.fix: HOSTBEAT already carries inputAck (u32, "all events with evSeq <= this are applied"). Use it: the Mac retransmits its highest-evSeq event (plus stateFlags and position) on a 10 ms timer until inputAck >= that evSeq, giving up after ~300 ms. No new fields, no new packet type, ~15 lines on the Mac and nothing on the host. This also subsumes the R-repeat window entirely and lets R drop to 1.

findings.title: Every deadline in the design assumes a frame crosses the wire in under one frame period; on any rate-limited path an IDR does not, and three mechanisms fail together
findings.sequence: Connect over Wi-Fi with ~20 Mbps of real capacity (2.5 MB/s) at 2560x1600, 60 fps, bitrateKbps 20000. The host sends the session-start IDR, which at that target is 200-400 KB (the design's own arithmetic puts a P-frame at ~40 KB and states an IDR is 5-10x a P-frame). It takes 80-160 ms to cross the bottleneck. Now watch three specified rules fire in sequence: (a) FRAME CLOSURE — "25 ms since its first fragment -> close as damaged". 25 ms x 2.5 MB/s = 62 KB, so only 15-30% of the fragments have arrived. The frame is declared damaged. (b) THE PACER — it is supposed to be the loss response, but it spreads fragments over min(framePeriod, bytes/measuredRate) = min(16.7 ms, 160 ms) = 16.7 ms. The min() caps the spread at one frame period, so the pacer bursts 400 KB at an instantaneous 190 Mbps into a 20 Mbps pipe. It is a no-op for exactly the frames that need pacing. (c) TIER 1 — "SENDER honours a NACK only if nowUs - sentAtUs < oneFramePeriodUs". The NACK for fragment 3 is queued behind the remaining 300 KB and arrives at t>160 ms. Every NACK for a large frame is rejected. The Mac then sends REQUEST_IDR, the tier-4 damper allows one per 500 ms, and the host emits another 400 KB IDR into the same 20 Mbps link: 6.4 Mbps of pure wasted keyframe, forever. No first frame is ever displayed.
findings.consequence: The stream never starts over Wi-Fi, and never recovers from a reference-chain break over Wi-Fi, because tier 4 — the last resort and the only session-start path — is structurally undeliverable there. This is the classic keyframe storm, and the design makes it self-sustaining because the wasted IDRs are themselves the congestion. Note the same arithmetic holds after the bitrate controller drops to its 2 Mbps floor on any path: at 250 KB/s the 25 ms timer admits 6 KB.
findings.fix: Three one-line changes, all in the same direction: (1) close a frame 25 ms after its LAST received fragment, not its first — an idle timeout, not a total timeout, which is the standard reassembly rule and is correct for any frame size; (2) drop the min() — pace at bytes/measuredRate with no framePeriod cap; (3) make the tier-1 sender deadline the frame's own display deadline (captureUs + one frame period + the current one-way delay estimate), not a flat oneFramePeriodUs since transmission.

findings.title: The transport counter resets to zero on every epoch bump, but the loss detector, the NACK space and the retransmit ring all assume it is monotonic
findings.sequence: Start a session. Ten minutes later the host's rekey timer fires. Per nonce clause (1), "the sender CASes to (epoch+1, counter=0)". The host's counter goes 1,499,999 -> 0 (at 2500 pps the 10-minute timer always fires long before the 2^31 threshold, so this is the normal path, not an edge case). Meanwhile sequencingAndLoss states the counter is "monotonic across every packet the sender emits whatever its type. This is the loss detector and the NACK/retransmit index." Three things break at once: (a) the gap classifier "highestCounter >= S + 8" sees the sequence restart and either declares a 1.5-million-packet gap or treats every new-epoch packet as ancient; (b) the NACK entry is [u48 startCounter][u8 run] with NO epoch field, so a NACK naming counter 5 is now ambiguous between two live epochs; (c) the sender's ring is ring[counter & 511] validated by "ring[counter & 511].counter == counter" with no epoch stored, so that ambiguous NACK matches the wrong epoch's entry and the sender retransmits a ten-minute-old sealed video fragment. It authenticates (epoch e-1 is still live for one second) and is then silently dropped by e-1's replay window, so the real repair never happens and the loss is never re-reported ("NACKs a declared-lost counter AT MOST ONCE"). FEEDBACK's rxCounter u48 "highest transport counter accepted" also goes backwards, which the bitrate controller's rxPackets/lostPackets accounting reads.
findings.consequence: A visible glitch plus a burst of useless NACK traffic and rejected repairs every 10 minutes of every session, in both directions, with the two directions bumping on independent timers so it happens twice. It is the hardest class of bug to diagnose because it is periodic, it only appears in long sessions, and the crypto is working perfectly throughout.
findings.fix: Do not reset the counter on an epoch bump. Keep the 48-bit counter monotonic per direction for the life of the session and let the epoch change only the key and the nonce fixed field. Nonce uniqueness is untouched — clause (2) already proves K(d,e) != K(d,e+1) and F(d,e) != F(d,e+1), so a repeated i would be harmless anyway — and 2^48 at 2500 pps is 3570 years, so counter exhaustion is not a concern. This also deletes the CAS, the permanently-zero guard band in bits 55..48, and the per-epoch replay window, which is a net simplification of the most safety-critical code in the design.

findings.title: The receiver is required to decide which frame a MISSING counter belonged to, which the design explicitly states it cannot do
findings.sequence: Suffer a 300 ms Wi-Fi stall (power save, channel scan, an AP beacon miss). 750 counters go missing at once. Now apply the specified NACK rule: "RECEIVER NACKs a declared-lost counter AT MOST ONCE, and only if the frame it would repair has not passed its deadline." The receiver never saw those 750 packets, so it does not know whether they carried VIDEO, AUDIO or HOSTBEAT, let alone which frameId — and the design says so in as many words: "the receiver never needs to know which frame a lost datagram belonged to." The deadline test is therefore unimplementable, and the same hole silently disables two other rules: DISCARDABLE suppression ("the receiver does not report loss for it, does not NACK it" — it cannot know the lost packet was discardable) and the "is this worth repairing" judgement generally. With no way to suppress, the receiver NACKs all 750. NACKs go out 8 per FEEDBACK at the 4 ms out-of-band floor: 2000 NACK slots per second, so 375 ms of feedback carrying nothing but requests the sender will reject on its own deadline test. Repeat on every stall.
findings.consequence: Every transient stall produces a self-inflicted burst of upstream traffic and sender-side ring lookups that can repair nothing, arriving exactly when the link has just proven it is in trouble. It also means DISCARDABLE — one of the two grafts justified as removing 'an entire class of pointless repair frames' — does nothing at all, because the flag lives in the video inner header of a packet that by definition did not arrive.
findings.fix: Bound NACK generation by the gap's own age, which the receiver does have: it records firstSeenAt for every gap. Never NACK a gap older than one frame period, and cap the outstanding NACK set to what a single FEEDBACK can carry, discarding the rest rather than queueing them. For DISCARDABLE, move the flag out of the lost packet: have HOSTBEAT (or a 1-bit field in the next frame's header) name the last discardable frameId, so the receiver can suppress against something it actually received.

findings.title: Closing a frame the instant a higher frameId appears turns benign reordering into repair frames, and then into permanent intra-refresh
findings.sequence: On Wi-Fi with A-MPDU aggregation, ~1% of datagrams arrive out of order — the design itself budgets for reordering up to 8 packets. Frame F is 28 fragments. Fragment 27 (carrying FRAME_END) is reordered behind fragment 0 of frame F+1. The rule "a fragment of a higher frameId arrives -> close as damaged" fires. Frame F is closed damaged 200 microseconds before its last fragment lands. The client sets REQUEST_LTR_RECOVERY and sends an immediate out-of-band FEEDBACK. The host burns a tier-2 repair frame on a frame that was never actually broken. Now escalate: tier 3 is entered on "three or more repairs needed within one second". At 60 fps and 1% reorder that is ~0.6 spurious closures per second, and any short burst of reordering trips three inside a second. Tier 3 costs 10-20% encoding efficiency and only exits after "3 s of zero loss" — which a reordering link never provides, because reordering keeps manufacturing closures.
findings.consequence: A link with reordering but no real loss settles permanently into intra-refresh at 10-20% worse quality, and the user sees a stream that is visibly softer on Wi-Fi than on Ethernet for no reason anyone can find in the loss counters (lostPackets will read zero). The 25 ms timer that was supposed to be the backstop never gets a chance to run.
findings.fix: Close F when a fragment of F+2 arrives, not F+1 — one extra open frame buffer, and it tolerates exactly the reordering depth the design already budgets for elsewhere. Keep the completeness test and the idle timer as the other two closure paths.

findings.title: Retransmissions and NACK-triggered feedback bypass the pacer, so the design adds load in proportion to loss
findings.sequence: Put the Mac on a congested 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi link at 40% loss. Video is 2500 pps, so 1000 packets/s are lost. The receiver NACKs each once; the sender honours what is inside its deadline. Retransmissions are explicitly exempt from the only congestion control in the design: "The pacer gates VIDEO only — never audio, input, feedback, control or retransmits." So the host now offers up to 40% MORE packets onto a link that is dropping 40%. Upstream, the out-of-band FEEDBACK floor is 4 ms rather than 16 ms, so the Mac's feedback rate quadruples to 250/s at the same moment. The bitrate controller reacts at x0.85 per 250 ms window, taking 3.5 s to reach the 2 Mbps floor — during which the retransmit multiplier is applied to a rate that is still 3-20 Mbps. And if the link's real capacity is below 2 Mbps, the controller pins at the floor and the retransmit amplification never stops, because the floor is absolute with no give-up state.
findings.consequence: Congestion collapse in the textbook shape: loss begets retransmits begets loss. Tier 1 was justified as free because 'a frame past its display deadline was going to be dropped either way' — that argues the retransmit adds no LATENCY, which is true, but says nothing about the bandwidth it adds, and bandwidth is what is scarce at 40% loss. The design has no mechanism that ever reduces retransmission in response to loss.
findings.fix: Route retransmits through the same pacer as fresh video, and debit them from the same measured send rate — a retransmitted byte must displace a fresh byte, not add to it. Two lines in the scheduler. Separately, when the controller sits at the 2 Mbps floor with loss still above 5% for 5 s, disable tier 1 entirely and let tier 3 carry the picture.

findings.title: The rewritten watchdog keys on HOSTBEAT, which is suppressed precisely when the stream is healthiest
findings.sequence: The design deletes the frame-based watchdog and replaces it: "session watchdog after 1 s of no frames (StreamSession.swift:184-225) -> REWRITTEN. It must key on HOSTBEAT arrival, not frame arrival." But HOSTBEAT is defined as "Sent every 100 ms whenever no VIDEO datagram went out in the last 100 ms." So: play a video full-screen on the host at 60 fps. VIDEO goes out continuously. Zero HOSTBEATs are emitted for the entire duration. The watchdog sees no HOSTBEAT for 1 s, declares the stream stalled, calls requestKeyframe() (StreamSession.swift:214-217), and after maxKeyframeRequests reports .lost — while a perfect 60 fps stream is on screen.
findings.consequence: The exact bug the rewrite was meant to prevent, inverted: instead of declaring a static window dead, it declares a moving window dead. And the intermediate action is requestKeyframe(), so on a busy stream it fires an IDR every second, which on a rate-limited path feeds straight into the IDR storm above.
findings.fix: Key the watchdog on the arrival of ANY authenticated host datagram (VIDEO, AUDIO, HOSTBEAT, PONG, PARAMSETS), not on HOSTBEAT specifically. One predicate change, and it is the natural rule anyway — the transport counter already gives a single liveness signal spanning all substreams, which is the design's own stated reason for having one counter.

findings.title: CAPTURE_LOST and a destroyed target window are signalled but nothing in the design consumes them
findings.sequence: Two paths, same ending. (a) The host GPU hits a TDR mid-session: the D3D device is removed, the WGC frame pool dies, no frames are produced. (b) The user closes the streamed application on the host, or minimises it (RESULTS.md open question 2: "WGC is expected to stop delivering frames"). In both cases the host sets hostFlags b4 CAPTURE_LOST and keeps emitting HOSTBEAT every 100 ms, because HOSTBEAT's trigger is 'no VIDEO went out', which is now permanently true. The Mac's watchdog sees HOSTBEAT arriving on schedule and reports .live. lastFrameId stops advancing, but nothing in the design consults it. The design defines the bit and never states a single rule that reads it — no host-side retry policy, no bound, no SESSION/STOP reason for 'the window you asked me to capture no longer exists', and no Mac-side UI state.
findings.consequence: The Mac window sits showing a frozen last frame indefinitely with the quality pill reporting a healthy stream. This is the same class of failure StreamSession.swift's own comment describes as the reason the watchdog exists at all — "stayed on screen indefinitely, with no spinner, no error and no way to tell a frozen stream from an application that simply was not redrawing" — reintroduced by making HOSTBEAT the liveness signal. Closing a window on the host is not an edge case; it is how a session normally ends.
findings.fix: Give CAPTURE_LOST a policy: the host retries capture-item creation for 2 s, then sends SESSION/STOP with reason=capture-lost (the STOP body is already a u8 reason with no values assigned) and tears down. On the Mac, CAPTURE_LOST is a terminal state that closes the streamed window with a message, distinct from ENCODER_IDLE. The bits already exist; only the two rules are missing.

findings.title: The primary bitrate signal poisons itself: captureUs wraps every 71.6 minutes and frameAgeUs is compared against a lifetime minimum
findings.sequence: captureUs is "u32 BE, host monotonic microseconds", so it wraps every 2^32 us = 4294.97 s = 71 minutes 35 seconds. Leave a session running that long. The Mac computes frameAgeUs = presented - captureUs; unless the subtraction is explicitly modular (nothing in the design says it is, and the PING/PONG path uses a u64 txUs from the same clock, so the natural offset estimator is built at a different width) frameAgeUs jumps by ~4295 s at the wrap. The design makes this the PRIMARY control input: "THE DELAY SIGNAL IS PRIMARY, NOT THE LOSS SIGNAL... multiplicative decrease x0.85 ... when frameAgeUs rises more than 30 ms above its session floor." x0.85 every 250 ms takes 20 Mbps to the 2 Mbps floor in 3.5 s. It never recovers, because the increase condition is "loss < 0.1% AND frameAgeUs is not trending up" and every post-wrap sample is 4295 s above the pre-wrap floor. Independently, and without any wrap: because the floor is a session-lifetime minimum, one lucky low sample in the first second pins it forever, so any sustained legitimate rise in path delay — the user moves a room away from the AP — produces permanent decrease pressure and the bitrate ratchets down and stays down.
findings.consequence: Guaranteed quality collapse 71.6 minutes into every long session, and a slow unexplained ratchet-down on any path whose delay baseline shifts. The user's report is 'it looks great for an hour and then goes to mush and never comes back', which is very hard to reproduce in a 5-minute test.
findings.fix: Compute frameAge with explicit wrapping u32 subtraction and discard any sample outside [0, 1 s] as a clock artefact; replace the lifetime 'session floor' with a sliding 10-second minimum. Both are standard delay-based congestion control practice and neither costs a wire byte. If you want the wrap gone entirely, widen captureUs to u48 — the video header has 3 spare bytes across psGen and the reserved space.

findings.title: audioSeq is u16 and wraps every 5 minutes 27 seconds, forcing a spurious Opus decoder reset
findings.sequence: One 5 ms Opus frame per datagram is 200 packets/s, so the u16 audioSeq wraps every 65536/200 = 327.7 s. Play audio for 5 minutes 28 seconds. audioSeq goes 65535 -> 0. The rule is "audioSeq gaps reset the Opus decoder so it does not interpolate across a hole"; unless the comparison is wrap-aware this reads as a 65535-frame gap and resets. The design widened evSeq from u16 to u32 for precisely this reason and said so — "a u16 wraps in about a minute of scrolling and forces wrap arithmetic into the host's dedup path" — then left audioSeq at u16 with the same hazard.
findings.consequence: An audible click roughly every five and a half minutes, plus HAS_PREV redundancy misbehaving across the boundary (the previous frame's audioSeq is audioSeq-1, which is 65535 when audioSeq is 0).
findings.fix: Widen audioSeq to u32. The AUDIO inner header has 2 reserved bytes at +10 doing nothing, so this costs zero wire bytes and keeps the header at 12.

findings.title: The 10-second agent-drop grace period is keyed to a sid but has no owner check, so a second Mac can take a session that is being held for the first
findings.sequence: Mac A is streaming. A's Wi-Fi blips and its agent TCP drops. Per reconnect case (b) the host holds "window locks and encoder state for a 10 s grace period keyed to sid". The agent socket is now free, so the one-client lock (main.cpp:3951-4021) no longer applies. At t+2 s Mac B — the same user's other Mac, holding the same 128-bit bearer token, which is the only credential — connects, authenticates, and sends {"cmd":"media","op":"open"}. Nothing in the design tests the reservation against the requester's identity, so B is granted a session while A's window locks are still held under A's sid. At t+8 s A reconnects and sends op:"resume" with its old sid; the agent is now busy with B and replies busy. A is locked out for the rest of B's session, and B is driving windows locked to A. Separately, the same case contradicts itself on lifetime: the 3 s host media expiry "stops the encoder, frees the session and zeroises the keys", which destroys the very "encoder state" the 10 s grace claims to hold, so a resume at t+5 s reattaches to an encoder that no longer exists.
findings.consequence: A Wi-Fi blip on one Mac can hand its streamed windows to another Mac and lock the original out, with no message to either user. Also a 1-in-256 flake underneath: sessTag is 8 bits and is described as the demux key during "the brief window where an old and a new session coexist" — a map keyed on it drops or evicts one of two coexisting sessions on collision.
findings.fix: Store the requesting client's auth identity (the proof from the auth v2 exchange is already per-connection) alongside the sid reservation and refuse a new media open from a different identity while the reservation is live. Reconcile the two lifetimes explicitly: the 3 s media expiry frees the encoder, the 10 s grace holds only window locks. Demux by full 32-bit sid, using sessTag only as the cheap prefilter it is described as.

findings.title: A TEXT input event longer than 255 bytes is unrepresentable, and INPUT has no fragmentation while DF is set
findings.sequence: Use a Japanese or Chinese IME on the Mac and commit a long phrase, or drive TEXT from any path that produces more than 255 bytes of UTF-8. The event framing is [u8 evType][u8 evLen][evLen bytes], so evLen cannot express it and the design specifies no continuation or chunking rule for 0x08 TEXT. Separately, the theoretical maximum INPUT datagram is 16 + 15 x (2 + 255) = 3871 bytes, well past the 1280-byte base MTU. Since IP_DONTFRAGMENT is set on the socket for MTU probing, an oversized INPUT is not fragmented — sendto returns EMSGSIZE or the datagram is dropped by the first hop, and INPUT has no retransmission at all, only redundancy.
findings.consequence: Silent, total loss of IME input above the threshold, on the one packet class the design states is order-critical and unrecoverable. The user sees nothing typed and no error.
findings.fix: Add a CONT bit to the TEXT event's first payload byte so a long commit spans consecutive evSeq events, and make the Mac's packetizer refuse to build an INPUT datagram larger than the current fragment size, splitting into consecutive datagrams instead. Both are Mac-side only; the host already applies events in evSeq order.

attacks.verdictOnDesign:
The cryptography is the strongest part of this document and I would ship it close to as written. The nonce construction is genuinely provably safe, clause (7) about never re-sealing a retransmit is the right invariant stated in the right place, the token-into-IKM decision buys backward secrecy against a token leak, and requiring auth v2 in the same commit is correct. My only crypto finding (#3) is not about the AEAD at all — it is that resetting the counter on rekey breaks the transport layered on top of it, and the fix makes the crypto simpler rather than weaker.

The failures cluster in one place, and it is the same place every time: this is a design calibrated for a gigabit LAN that treats Wi-Fi as a perturbation of that regime rather than a different regime. Almost every constant assumes a frame crosses the wire in less than one frame period — the 25 ms frame-closure timer, the min(framePeriod, ...) pacer, the one-frame-period tier-1 deadline, the 512-entry ring sized at 200 ms, the 8-packet reorder threshold. On a 20 Mbps Wi-Fi link an IDR takes 160 ms and all four are wrong simultaneously and in the same direction, which is how you get an IDR storm rather than a graceful degradation. The document is honest that "every quantitative claim here is arithmetic, not measurement" — but the arithmetic was done at 1 Gbps, and the section that talks about Wi-Fi (the pacer) is the one section whose formula has the inequality backwards.

The second cluster is smaller and easier: three or four places where a bit is defined and no rule consumes it (CAPTURE_LOST, DISCARDABLE, inputAck), and one place where the receiver is asked to make a decision using information the same document says it does not have. These read like the seams between the spine and the grafts, and finding #4 in particular is a straight incompatibility — design 1's retransmission scheme assumed a receiver that tracks frames, and it was grafted onto design 2's receiver that deliberately does not.

Two things I want to say in the design's favour, because they will matter when the bug reports come in. The build order is right: putting the cross-language crypto vectors at step 1 and the LTR encoder unknown at step 6 is exactly the sequencing I would want, and step 5's file-driven video source is the correct way to measure the transport without the encoder as a variable. And ltrHave is as good as the document claims — I went looking for a stale-slot race in it and could not construct one, because the "not named in damagedMask AND frameId <= lastGoodFrame" pair closes the hole that "CONFIRMED" alone would leave open.

Findings #1 and #2 I would block on. #1 because a single lost packet produces a stuck key with no recovery path and no timeout, which is the failure the requirements name explicitly and which the current code already has machinery to paper over. #2 because the product does not start over Wi-Fi. Everything else is fixable after step 5 produces real numbers, and several of the fixes (#3, #9, #10) are net simplifications.
